    E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists.
    • If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms.
    • I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists. They’ve also become a hot topic in online forums and parenting circles, where people constantly worry about kids on e-bikes going too fast, losing control or making poor choices. I’ve seen it myself on my city’s bike path—kids flying by and recklessly weaving past pedestrians and other cyclists.

    If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms. A JAMA study published in November 2026 looked at more than 13,000 injury visits for kids under 18 at six large U.S. children’s hospitals between 2023 and early 2026. E-bike injuries grew 33% per quarter over that stretch and e-scooter injuries grew 15% per quarter, compared with 2% for traditional bikes and 4% for traditional scooters. About a quarter of the e-bike injuries and nearly half of the e-scooter injuries involved kids under 12.

    I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr. Beth C. Natt, system medical director of pediatrics at Atlantic Health, and Dr. Zebulon J. Timmons, division chief of emergency medicine at Children’s Nebraska in Omaha, about what parents should weigh before buying one and how to keep kids safer if one is already in the garage.

    According to recent reports, “It mostly comes down to speed,” Natt notes. “Doubling the speed roughly quadruples the force in a crash.” Some e-bikes can top 25 mph, and Natt notes that e-bike crashes are far more likely to involve a car.

    In a recent development, timmons points to the rider as much as the bike. “Kids do not have the frontal lobe capacity and reaction time to make judgments at that speed,” he says. “You don’t take your young child to the batting cages and have them start at 80 mph.”.

    In the JAMA study, 17% of e-bike injuries led to a hospital stay, the highest share of any group of injuries, and 10% involved a brain injury, double the rate for regular bikes. Severe injuries, like those needing ICU care or surgery to fix a fracture, were twice as common on e-bikes, too (8% vs. 4%). Natt mostly sees broken wrists, arms and legs, plus head, face and dental injuries. Timmons sees a lot of open fractures, where the bone breaks through the skin. “Kids’ heads are bigger relative to their bodies, so they tend to hit head-first,” Natt says, “and a fracture through a growth plate can affect how a bone grows later.”.

    The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) indicates kids under 16 shouldn’t ride e-scooters and, citing Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance, no e-bikes for kids under 12. Timmons says kids 12 to 15 can ride a Class 1 e-bike with proper safety training and gear, and teens 16 and up can consider a Class 2, though many will still be safer on a Class 1. Natt is more conservative. “Most pediatric injury experts would say no throttle-powered e-bike or e-scooter before about 16, and some argue for 18,” she says.

    A child is ready, Natt says, if they can handle a regular bike confidently in traffic, follow the rules when you’re not around, wear a helmet without reminders and judge how fast cars are coming. “Most kids don’t have that judgment until at least their teens,” she notes.

    Class 1 e-bikes are pedal-assist only, up to 20 mph. Class 2 adds a throttle, still capped at 20 mph. Class 3 is pedal-assist up to 28 mph, and many states restrict it to riders 16 and older. For kids, choose Class 1 and skip the throttle, Natt indicates, and avoid “e-motos” sold as e-bikes, since they go much faster. Both doctors note a regular pedal bike is still the safest choice for most kids.

    There’s no federal minimum age for e-bikes, and more than half of states set age limits for Class 3 models, so check your state and town’s rules before you buy.

    Industry observers note that timmons indicates a standard bike helmet is fine up to about 15 mph. From 15 to 25 mph, he recommends a helmet certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard, and above 25 mph, a motorcycle or moped helmet. A full-face helmet adds protection for the face and jaw, Natt says, and any helmet should be replaced after a crash.

    Keeping it on is another matter. Timmons indicates fewer than 25% of kids treated in pediatric emergency departments were wearing a helmet when they crashed, and many take them off once they’re out of a parent’s sight. Make wearing a helmet a non-negotiable, and let friends and neighbors know to keep an eye on your child. If they’re spotted without the helmet, the bike goes away.

    Sources indicate that after the helmet, wrist guards and gloves help most because broken wrists are so common, Natt says. Front and rear lights plus reflective clothing help drivers see your child. Timmons recommends that kids wear closed-toe shoes (“No Crocs”), and for teens 16 and up on a Class 2, motorcycle-style long pants and sleeves.

    Any head injury or neck pain after an e-bike or e-scooter crash should be checked in the emergency room, Timmons notes. Natt says to go if your child passed out, even briefly, or keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, a seizure, weakness or numbness, belly pain, a limb that looks bent or can’t bear weight, or a deep cut or facial or dental injury.

    It has been revealed that watch for “handlebar injuries,” too, when the handlebars turn sideways and strike the chest or belly. “This mechanism causes all the force to be delivered to a small area and can cause significant internal injuries,” Timmons says. A handlebar-shaped bruise on the chest or abdomen means a trip to the ER. Once there, tell the care team what kind of e-bike your child was riding and whether they wore a helmet, Natt says.

    If the e-bike or e-scooter isn’t right for your child’s age, consider exchanging it, Timmons notes, or look for a community buy-back program. “This last trauma season was the worst one in my career and that was largely driven by e-bike/scooter injuries,” he says.

    It has been revealed that “These are motor vehicles, not toys,” Natt indicates. “A crash at e-bike speed can look more like a motorcycle injury than a bike injury.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    Throughout October, we are throwing our support behind the mission to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month, an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and recognize the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. With around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, we know it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming, and one group that understands this more than most is The Cat Network in Miami, Florida.

    Sources indicate that founded in 1995, The Cat Network is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization supported by more than 2,500 volunteers and donors, helping community cats, stray, abandoned, and homeless cats throughout South Florida while supporting the people who care for them. Through education, low-cost spay/neuter services, adoption assistance, and advocacy, the organization works to humanely reduce cat overpopulation and improve the lives of cats and the communities they live in.

    The Cat Network is dedicated to humanely reducing cat overpopulation in South Florida through five core pillars: education, sterilization, adoption, advocacy, and humane public policy. Our story begins more than 30 years agoâ¦.

    Sources indicate that in July 1995, the City Manager of Miami Beach contracted with a commercial trapper, Humane Animal Removal, to trap and euthanize the cityâs feral cats, with a bounty of $35.00 for each cat trapped and killed. When this became public, a local and national outcry ensued, and the media had a field day. The Cat Network, still in its infancy, helped organize local opposition to the trap-kill plan. Susan Fleming, president of The Cat Network and a Miami Beach resident, was instrumental in negotiating with the City to institute TNR instead. With help from Animal Controlâs mobile animal clinic and SoBe spay/neuter certificates, we convinced the City to implement the more humane approach of TNR.

    The following year, we began our spay/neuter certificate program with participating veterinary clinics, the first of which was Galloway Animal Clinic. Since 1995, we've helped sterilize more than 122,000 cats and assisted in the adoption of more than 24,000 cats.

    Sources indicate that what makes us unique is our comprehensive approach. Rather than simply responding to the symptoms of overpopulation, we focus on preventing future litters while helping cats in need. Our programs include the Miami Meow Mobile, low-cost spay/neuter vouchers, adoption referrals through an extensive foster network, public education, and advocacy for Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR) as the most humane and effective way to manage community cat populations.

    Industry observers note that one of our biggest challenges is simply the sheer number of cats needing help. Because South Florida has warm weather year-round, kitten season never truly ends. This creates an ongoing demand for spay and neuter services, foster homes, adoptions, and community education. Every day we receive calls from residents who have discovered kittens, injured cats, or growing community cat colonies.

    Industry observers note that there really isn't an "off season" for cat rescue here, so our volunteers and veterinary programs stay busy throughout the entire year. Preventing unwanted litters through early sterilization is one of the most effective ways to reduce this constant cycle.

    In a recent development, funding is another ongoing challenge. Keeping our veterinary programs affordable requires significant community support, and the costs of medical supplies, equipment, and operations continue to rise.

    People can make an enormous difference by:.

    Donating to support our programs.

    Becoming a volunteer or foster caregiver.

    Spaying and neutering their own pets.

    Helping community cats through TNR.

    Sharing our educational resources and adoptable cats on social media.

    Becoming a member of The Cat Network.

    Every donation, volunteer hour, and shared post helps save lives.

    Over the past 30 years, The Cat Network has become one of South Florida's leading organizations dedicated to reducing cat overpopulation. Sterilizing more than 122,000 cats and helping over 24,000 cats find homes are milestones that represent countless lives saved.

    We're especially proud of the Miami Meow Mobile, which has dramatically increased access to affordable veterinary care, and our long-standing network of volunteers and foster caregivers who make our adoption program possible. Together, these programs have helped thousands of residents become part of the solution while improving animal welfare throughout South Florida.

    Recent findings suggest that the Miami Meow Mobile is a fully equipped veterinary clinic designed specifically for cats. Originally envisioned in 2001 and launched in 2005, it was created to make affordable veterinary care accessible to more people throughout the community.

    Industry observers note that today, the Meow Mobile provides low-cost spay and neuter surgeries, vaccinations, testing, microchipping, parasite treatments, and basic wellness services. Originally designed as a traveling clinic, it presently operates from a fixed location in Kendall, allowing us to serve a large number of cats efficiently and safely.

    The Meow Mobile remains one of our signature programs because every surgery performed helps prevent future litters and reduces shelter overcrowding throughout South Florida.

    Our Spay/Neuter Certificate Program partners with participating veterinarians throughout South Florida. Residents can purchase discounted certificates that cover sterilization surgery, a rabies vaccination, and ear tipping for community cats.

    Sources indicate that this partnership expands access to affordable veterinary care beyond our own clinic. If someone discovers a stray or community cat in their neighborhood, the voucher program provides an affordable pathway to have that cat sterilized before additional litters are born.

    By working together with local veterinary clinics, we're able to reach far more cats than we could alone and give residents practical tools to help solve the community cat problem.

    Working with cats means no two days are ever alike. Volunteers have rescued kittens from engine compartments, construction sites, shopping centers, and backyard sheds. Every rescue brings its own surprisesâand often a few scratches and plenty of memorable stories.

    Recent findings suggest that the resilience of these cats never stops amazing us. Watching frightened community kittens transform into affectionate family pets is one of the most rewarding experiences we witness over and over again.

    Sources indicate that every cat that is sterilized prevents countless future kittens from being born into homelessness. Every adoption changes two livesâthe cat's and the family's.

    Knowing that thousands of volunteers, donors, veterinarians, and community members are working together toward the same goal makes every success even more meaningful.

    As we celebrate over 30 years of service, our goal remains the same: continuing to expand access to affordable spay and neuter serviceswhile working toward a future where no healthy or treatable cat is euthanized simply because there are too many homeless animals.

    We continue to strengthen our community partnerships, grow volunteer involvement, support foster caregivers, and educate the public about responsible pet ownership and Trap-Neuter-Return practices.

    Anyone interested in getting involved can learn more by visiting TheCatNetwork.org. There they can become a member, volunteer, foster cats, adopt, donate, or schedule services through the Miami Meow Mobile.

    #8977. Breaking: How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1443 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.
    • Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged?
    • According to recent reports, all kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.

    Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged? Does a dose of antibiotics require two adults, one to immobilize and one to administer the medication? And potentially a change of clothing for you and/or your child afterwards? If so, you might have a sensitive sick kid.

    According to recent reports, all kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage. And it always seems that the kids who struggle the most are the ones who will inevitably catch every bug. Unfortunately, my family is a regular fixture at our pediatrician’s office and our local CVS pharmacy as a result.

    Medication administration is not easy for a lot of parents. And during illnesses such as the flu, strep throat, or ear infections, a whole host of medications may be recommended for pain, fever reduction, or coughs. While some of these medications are available in “kid-friendly” flavors, it doesn’t mean that your sensitive kiddo is going to agree with that assessment. Board-certified pediatrician Dr. Lauren Hughes recommends that parents choose their battles, because many medications, while helpful in ideal circumstances, aren’t critical for recovery.

    In a recent development, “There is no real good data for vapor rubs or OTC cough meds in kids under 6 years. Honestly, my favorite cough medicine [for] children is just a spoonful of honey,” states Hughes. “When it comes to things like ibuprofen and acetaminophen, these are helpful for controlling pain and discomfort, which can often help the child feel better so they will continue drinking and staying hydrated. However, a fever itself is not harmful in children over 60 days with normal immune systems.”.

    Lindsay McHugh, DNP, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and co-founder of Resting Roo, recommends that parents of children who have difficulty taking medications experiment with other ways to ease symptoms. “You [can] try heating packs to alleviate pain or ice packs, or if they have a stuffy, you could warm that up in the microwave, and they could hold it on a certain spot,” McHugh says, “[For fever] a warm bath or a lukewarm or even a cool bath, whatever feels right to your child at the time… to make them as comfortable as possible.”.

    It has been revealed that both McHugh and Hughes say taking the full course of antibiotics if prescribed needs to be parents’ priority. “If we don’t take [all] the antibiotics, then they could potentially build a resistance,” states McHugh. “If they build a resistance, then we have even sicker kids for even longer.”.

    In a recent development, unfortunately, antibiotics — which can taste disgusting and/or have gritty textures — can be the biggest medication battle. Hughes has the following recommendations:.

    An absolute game changer in our family has been my daughter learning to swallow pills. Now I wish we had tried it much sooner. McHugh claims that while some 3-year-olds might be ready, parents usually can start trying with their children at age 4 or 5. “[You can start] practicing with certain foods that are somewhat pill-shaped, not too big, something soft… like a pea,” says McHugh, “[And say], ‘Let’s practice trying to not chew your pea. Let’s practice trying to swallow it.’ Practice outside of being sick. So then when they are sick, then it’s not so foreign.”.

    Once my daughter got the hang of it, it changed everything: When she needed antibiotics a couple months later, the pediatrician was able to prescribe pills she could swallow.

    According to recent reports, our entire family has a history of sensitive skin, allergies, and skin ailments like eczema. These seem to frequently coexist in individuals with other sensory sensitivities. Both my daughter and I, for example, can react to the adhesive in some Band-Aids. Now we use Band-Aids for Sensitive Skin for her or, alternatively, sensitive skin tape and non-stick gauze for protecting and healing cuts and injuries.

    While it’s ideal to only use products that you know your child likes and doesn’t react to, sometimes you need to make a change or try something upcoming for a symptom or illness you haven’t encountered before. For items with topical application, McHugh recommends checking out Environmental Working Group’s Skin Deep database to research products that may include ingredients you know your child is allergic or sensitive to or might cause a reaction.

    Industry observers note that mcHugh recommends trying out new topical items on an area of the body where your child is the least sensitive (which will be different for every child), while they are healthy. “Pick a 1x1 or a 2x2 inch square, and try the product, a little bit at a time. I would…see how they [and] how their skin responds,” says McHugh, “So maybe on day two or three we do this whole leg [and] see if that’s not too overwhelming from skin sensitivity as well as the smell or feel.”.

    Since my daughter and I are both sensitive to smells, I also have her smell-test products in the store aisle before we buy.

    It has been revealed that since I have a kiddo who is sensitive to touch and texture even when she is feeling 100%, standard oral thermometers have pretty much been a no-go since she was an infant, and temporal thermometers can be tricky on a sweaty kid who doesn’t like to be touched. A no-touch forehead thermometer gets a quick read without any contact, and one with a silent mode lets you take overnight temps without waking them.

    Illness can be especially tricky for younger children who can’t (or won’t) blow their noses. But Hughes claims it is especially critical for infants who are under six months who are still exclusively breast- or bottle-fed: When they’re congested, they can’t breathe while feeding and are likely to become dehydrated.

    Sources indicate that for using inhalers, nasal aspirators, and nasal saline, Hughes recommends the following hold: “The adult sits down with their legs spread in a V. They put the child’s head up between their legs and then place the child’s arms under their thighs. The parent then crosses their shins/ankles over the child’s legs to hold them in place. This allows the parent to have both hands free while the child is immobilized without harming them.”.

    Here are some other tips for treatment of congestion, drainage, and coughs:.

    Illnesses and injuries can be exhausting for sensitive kids and their parents. And it can be easy to start feeling guilty for having to force your child to take medicine or do some other treatment that was uncomfortable, even if it was best for them and helped them feel better in the long term. This can be especially challenging if you are trying to teach your children about bodily autonomy and boundaries.

    McHugh recommends that parents try to be clear before these moments about what you are going to have to do, that you are taking care of them, they are safe, and that you know that it may be uncomfortable, painful, or taste yucky.

    According to recent reports, “[After] I would offer empathy [and] validate their experience,” indicates McHugh, “And then I would say, ‘I know in the past we've talked about body autonomy, body safety. And it feels like Mommy and Daddy broke that. I’m sorry that we did that… However, we have to take care of you, and your safety is our number one priority.’”.

    When our kids are sick or have an injury, it’s a high-stress time. You’re worried about your child, but you’re also worried about doing the right thing and taking care of them the right way. And sometimes you need to do what you need to do, whether it is accepting help from those around you, asking for a break, or yes, bribing your child to cooperate with some part of their care.

    Sources indicate that “When your child isn’t feeling good, you’re already on edge. It’s most appropriate to treat [them] so that they don’t get sicker, and we want to take care of our babies and do everything we can. And if it takes a couple extra popsicles…that’s perfectly okay,” reflects McHugh, “Don’t forget to take care of yourself; it’s the last thing on the list. But [sometimes] you just need a little break to go to the bathroom and cry, because it was awful.”.

    #8975. Jennifer Garner reveals how Once Upon a Farm became a $724 million tech giant without sacrificing its values at Motherly’s State of Motherhood event

    Jennifer Garner reveals how Once Upon a Farm became a $724 million tech giant without sacrificing its values at Motherly’s State of Motherhood event

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.
    • That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.
    • Sources indicate that the conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.

    That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.

    Sources indicate that the conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research. Every year since 2018, we’ve polled thousands of moms (more than 60,000 in fact!) for our annual State of Motherhood survey. And every year, moms have told us they’re scaling back at work and having fewer children than they’d prefer, but they’re still feeling isolated and overwhelmed. In 2025, 70% of moms stated motherhood is lonelier than expected and in 2026, 42% felt more burned out than in the previous year.

    Industry observers note that “The truth is that our expectations of what it means to be a good mom changed faster than the systems built around to support her, and Gen Z moms are running into that gap even earlier,” said Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi in her opening remarks. “But none of us should have to sacrifice our sanity, our careers, our identities to have children, and no mother should have to carry it alone.”.

    Leaders from organizations at the Clinton Foundation, the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, the ACLU, and the Vote Mama Foundation, joined together with executives at JP Morgan, Pfizer, Coterie, IKEA, and Paramount, to hear from women who are working tirelessly to create a world where moms feel supported, connected, and respected.

    That included actress Jennifer Garner, who talked about her work as an ambassador for Save the Children and as co-founder of organic children’s nutrition manufacturer Once Upon a Farm.

    Garner kicked off the event in a fireside chat that touched on everything from finding community as a mom to the importance of advocating for children and families.

    “Every kid deserves healthy, real food, an education, and parents who have a roof over their heads, food in their bellies, and time and space and energy and support to love their kids,” she stated. Traveling around the country for her work with Save the Children, she described seeing families stretch food-bank, WIC, and SNAP resources to feed their children.

    That’s why Once Upon a Farm worked hard to become the first WIC-certified organization offering organic refrigerated baby food, she mentioned. The company is now WIC-certified in 22 states. For Garner, it’s about dignity and choice: families using public benefits should be able to access high-quality food.

    It’s all baked in, pun intended, to the organization’s social mission to “drive systemic change in childhood nutrition for a happier, healthier, more equitable world,” Garner indicates. In 2021, the company transitioned its corporate structure from an LLC to a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which legally requires it to balance profitability with its social and environmental impact. It’s a challenging path for a business to pursue, which is why there are fewer than 20 publicly-traded PBCs, and Once Upon a Farm is the only one focused on kids. Towards those goals, Garner said, the company has donated a million meals to kids in rural America, and it pays a premium for produce “so that the people who are growing and picking our food are recruited ethically, and have a say in their safety and what their workday looks like.”.

    When it comes to balancing the demands of her multi-hyphenite life with motherhood, Garner didn’t hold back. On her non-negotiables, she joked, “I work out every day… unless I don’t. I read every night until I fall asleep… one page or none. I go to church… when I can. My kids come first… except for weeks where it’s crazy and I tell them they come first from afar.”.

    Finding the right balance changes day by day, Garner mentioned. She assesses who needs her most in a given moment, including herself. “You get to choose moment to moment what you do and what your family needs,” she said to the moms in the room.

    She also encouraged moms to come together to help defeat the loneliness that Motherly’s data revealed. “We’re literally meant to be in community,” she described. “When my second was born, I joined a baby group for second-time moms, and that is the most active group chat on my phone to this day.”.

    Plus, she added, small groups of committed moms have the power to make real change.

    It has been revealed that “We all love our babies the same. And when you realize that, that every mother in the world loves their baby the way you love yours, which seems impossible, but it is true, that also connects you to every other mother,” she mentioned. “And then you feel like, how can I help every other mother who doesn’t have the advantages I have?”.

    In a recent development, next up was a panel about the state of motherhood in 2026, breaking down Motherly’s data showing that moms are increasingly burned out, and figuring out fixes to help. Featuring some of the most influential women working to make the United States a better place for families, the panelists pointed out that burnout is a structural problem — not an individual failure — and that collective action can turn broad public support for family policies into change.

    In a recent development, “I think motherhood in America is impossible by design,” mentioned Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, a national non-profit organization working to advance paid leave and affordable childcare for working families. “Why does the school day end at 2:30 and the workday end at six? Why do we pay more for our childcare than our mortgage? Why do one out of four women go back to work two weeks after having a baby?”.

    Recent findings suggest that lauren Smith Brody, the founder of The Fifth Trimester and co-founder of Chamber of Mothers, said she’s optimistic that federal lawmakers will soon advance legislation to help moms across the country, including paid family leave, affordable childcare for all, and measures to improve maternal health outcomes. “I feel a lot of hope as we walk into these offices on Capitol Hill and we make a lot of behind the scenes connections between Democratic offices and Republican offices, because guess what? They actually do want many of the same things,” she said. “Moms are top of the list. They know that our voting power is unmatched. They know that they need us. They know that we voted them in and can vote them out.”.

    In a recent development, “I am telling you standing right here, [affordable] childcare and paid leave will get passed in 2029 within the first hundred days,” Saujani remarked. “I don’t care who is elected president because we are getting this done.”.

    It’s all about moms coming together to hold leaders accountable, stated Ailen Arreaza, the executive director of the national nonprofit parents organization ParentsTogether. “Moms often feel it’s our sole responsibility to protect our kids, and feel shame when we think we’ve failed — especially when it comes to technology,” she said. “One of the best ways that we can hold companies accountable is by sharing our stories. We do a lot of work with parents who have lost children to significant tech, and their stories are so powerful,” she said. “That also helps with the shame. When we talk to each other about what we are struggling with, what we are facing, that shame evaporates.”.

    Sources indicate that michelle Jawando, the CEO of Omidyar Network, a philanthropy organization working to foster responsible technology and AI development, said she’s encouraged by the fact that the mistakes of the “move-fast-and-break-things” era in Silicon Valley are providing a roadmap for more responsible tech development going forward. “I believe that everything that happened in that proceeding era gives us an opportunity to get AI right,” she said, pointing to California, which recently passed the strongest AI companion chatbot legislation in the country.

    The morning’s final panel, moderated by the host of Motherly’s new podcast, Daniela Gysler-Wood, provided practical ways mothers can protect their physical and mental well-being.

    Dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell, a board certified family medicine physician and the author of the upcoming book How to Talk to Your Doctor, encouraged moms to keep seeking answers if they’re feeling unwell. Her advice? If a clinician says you are fine but you do not feel fine, say, “I understand that you think I’m fine, but I’m not. What are the next steps?”.

    She also suggested asking, “What three to five possibilities are on your working list?” This helps you understand the range of possibilities if your doctor is focused on just one diagnosis.

    It has been revealed that when it comes to getting enough rest, celebrate the small wins, stated Megan Holm, the women’s sleep research lead at sleep technology firm Eight Sleep. “Sleep when you can, and you don’t need to check off everything on your to-do list in order to put your head on the pillow. You can take a 30-minute nap,” she said.

    Industry observers note that “I think we’ve all just accepted that exhaustion is part of motherhood, and I don’t think that’s where we should be,” said Victoria Thain Gioia, the co-founder and CEO of Perelel, an OB/GYN-founded and doctor-formulated vitamin and supplement brand. “To get through the day and stay sane, and to take care of small children, and do your job, you need to be nutritionally sufficient, not depleted. So while it can sometimes be overhyped, the conversation about protein, collagen, lactoferrin and nutrients that can actually support your energy [is notable]. We really need to focus on care for mom beyond just pregnancy and postpartum.”.

    According to recent reports, when it comes to protecting our mental well-being, the panelists encouraged moms to let go of guilt and connect with other parents. “Check in on your friends, nurture your friendships, don’t ask everything of your partner or your spouse, and ask for help,” said Elise Hu, the host of TED Talks Daily, a flagship podcast from TED Conferences. “Asking for help doesn’t just benefit you, the person who needs the help, it also benefits the helper because think about all the times that you have been asked for advice or counsel. That’s such a tribute to you, right? Because somebody is saying to you, ‘I trust you and I trust your advice and I trust your counsel.’ It nurtures the connection on both ends, not only for the helpee, but also the helper.”.

    The moms in the room didn’t just leave with actionable advice and encouragement – although there was plenty on tap – they also took home a Happ Paige Mini full of goodies, including Once Upon a Farm snacks, Perelel Collagen+ Defense Supplements, Shiseido Sun Protector Clear Stick Sunscreen, Then I Met You Cleansing Balm, Ursa Major Golden Hour Recovery Cream, Merit Shade Slick, and the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle.

    According to recent reports, guests also got a chance to try out a mini version of Eight Sleep’s pod, an intelligent mattress cover that uses built-in biometric sensors to track your sleep and automatically adjust its temperature. “In May, we released pregnancy mode, which is automatic temperature support to support women as they go through pregnancy and up to 24 weeks postpartum,” said Holm, Eight Sleep’s women’s research lead, during the second panel. “As you grow a child, the environment around you feels really hot and uncomfortable. So we automatically make sure that when you can rest, and even if it’s not for eight hours every night, you’re comfortable.”.

    Recent findings suggest that and bestselling author Loryn Brantz greeted guests as they walked into the room, signing free copies of her fresh release, I Am a Spicy Nugget, as well as copies of her New York Times bestseller, Poems of Parenting. Some lucky guests also received a signed print.

    Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi closed out the day with a call to action for all of the “incredible, powerful, influential” women in the room: “From all these conversations, I heard over and over that we need community, and that community is power, substantial or small,” she began. “We need advocates, people who fight relentlessly for the care, the policies and the respect that moms deserve. And we need storytellers, people who show the real picture of this journey at every stage without judgment.”.

    That’s where Motherly can play a powerful role going forward, she noted.

    It has been revealed that “Motherly is growing from a trusted resource into an active community online and off,” she explained. “What does that mean in practice? It means we’re showing up in her group chat. We’re in her feed with a slate of new vertical video highlights that I’m really excited about. We’re in her earbuds with a new podcast. And we’re popping up in her neighborhood with our new hyper local event series, coming to a neighborhood near you so that moms can find the people where they are.”.

    The real must-haves, how to prevent diaper rash from day one, and where your budget actually matters.

    Bringing a baby home is exhausting, but at least you know how to prepare. Or do you? Every time you turn your phone on, there’s a latest product being advertised that your baby absolutely must have. News flash: they don’t. Babies aren’t influencers. They don’t need a 12-step skincare routine, and you don’t have to buy a wipe warmer to be a good parent.

    Pediatric guidance necessitates a much shorter list than your feed does. Here’s what you actually need to focus on.

    Recent findings suggest that having a newborn is chaotic enough (IYKYK); your checklist shouldn’t add to it. File these under real must-haves:.

    That’s it, truly. Everything else is a nice-to-have you can just buy later.

    Recent findings suggest that you’ll be changing a lot of diapers every day, so one of the most key things you can do is establish a good diapering routine. This is what you need within arm’s reach:.

    It has been revealed that it all comes down to what’s in the wipe and how reactive your baby’s skin is. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises avoiding fragrances, dyes, and parabens on infant skin, so that's a good place to start.

    The bottom line: For most newborns, a fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe is just fine. Don't worry about water wipes unless your baby's skin reacts to everything.

    It has been revealed that most diaper rash is the byproduct of moisture and friction, so the best way to prevent it is to establish a good changing routine. Here’s what the AAP advises:.

    Call your pediatrician if the rash:.

    It goes without saying that this checklist doesn’t replace your pediatrician’s advice. For questions or concerns about a lingering diaper rash, call them.

    Babies are not cheap! You'll be blowing through roughly 240 to 360 diapers a month. Here are some ways you can save:.

    Prioritize fit and leak protection.

    It has been revealed that make your diaper budget work for you. Fewer leaks and blowouts mean fewer outfit changes (and fewer middle-of-the-night sheet swaps). So, the convenience alone will pay for itself. You don’t even have to trade up to a premium line to get it: Mainstream Pampers lines like Swaddlers and Baby Dry cover the pediatric-aligned basics. Store-brand diapers offer a lower-cost option for budget-conscious parents.

    If your baby's skin isn't super reactive, there’s no need to splurge on specialty wipes. A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive-skin wipe'll do the trick.

    It has been revealed that weigh a subscription vs. buying separately.

    Here are five picks, drilled down by category:.

    What are the best newborn care essentials to buy before the baby arrives?

    Stick to the basics: a safe sleep surface, an infant car seat, diapering supplies (diapers, wipes, barrier cream, and a changing surface), a few onesies, and whatever your feeding blueprint requires. Everything else can wait.

    Should I get sensitive-skin wipes or water wipes for newborn diaper changes?

    Fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipes meet pediatric guidance for everyday newborn use. Water wipes are an extra-cautious option for babies who have eczema-prone or very reactive skin.

    What newborn essentials are best for preventing diaper rash from day one?

    Two non-negotiables: Change diapers frequently and use a zinc-oxide or petrolatum-based barrier cream. A well-fitting, absorbent diaper helps too.

    Should I prioritize premium diapers or sensitive wipes in my newborn essentials budget?

    According to recent reports, prioritize diaper fit and leak protection first, since that’s what keeps moisture off skin (and blowouts off clothes). Then save on wipes: A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe covers most babies without specialty pricing.

    Is a diaper subscription bundle or buying essentials separately a better value for newborns?

    Industry observers note that this is really a convenience-vs-flexibility call. Diaper subscription bundles offer discounts the more you buy and can spare you store runs. Buying separately lets you switch sizes as your baby grows — which happens fast in the newborn stage!

    What are the best newborn care essentials to buy in 2026?

    Industry observers note that the same ones as always. The core list (sleep surface, car seat, diapering, clothes, and feeding) hasn’t changed in 2026; there are just more options. You still need a snug/leakproof diaper, fragrance-free wipes, a zinc-oxide barrier cream, and a portable changing pad.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.

    In a recent development, my Nana was not a good cook. Not really. Her food was always basic. Good, but basic. I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself. She was Irish and had about 12 things she knew how to cook and they were basically all holiday menu-specific. She could do up a roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy. A bag of coleslaw with a bottle of creamy dressing tossed in. She bought those little grocery store dinner rolls and popped them in the oven to warm as my Grandpa carved the turkey, his only chance to shine in the winter season as the barbeque was no longer an option.

    Industry observers note that her baking though, now that was good. A bit better than good by ‘80s standards since the Great British Baking Show didn’t exist. She made excellent sticky buns and little donuts she shook in paper bags of cinnamon and sugar while they were piping hot. She baked birthday cakes for all of the grandchildren, chocolate and peanut butter, or strawberry cream, or white cake with jam in the middle.

    Industry observers note that most of all, she baked raisin bread. Loaf after loaf of raisin bread for everyone she knew. We’ve never found the recipe in the two decades that she has been gone, and it is the thing her whole family misses the most. The dark, molasses smell of it. A nod to her Nova Scotian heritage. Sturdy enough to toast if you cut your morning slab extra thick. Sturdy enough for a great massive smear of peanut butter too. A singular flavor I will miss forever.

    Her raisin bread and cinnamon buns and chocolate cakes were not the things that drew us all to her kitchen. Her turkey wasn’t even really moist enough to have us all clamoring for late night sandwiches, and yet there we stood. Every year. Daughters and sons, grandchildren, friends. Some of us in pajamas, others in track pants to accommodate our food babies. My quiet Grandpa hovering around the periphery, hoping someone would make him a plate of food. We came for the sandwich but mostly we came for her. My Nana. A short, bossy, contrary matriarch who made messes, made toast with marmalade on cold mornings, made cup after cup of tea left too long on the stove.

    She made me want to be just like her. To call my loves back to my own kitchen. To make people feel welcome and loved and relaxed and just seen, all the time she was seeing us out of the corner of her eye. “What’s wrong?” she’d ask me as she was kneading cinnamon-scented dough for her raisin bread, all casual and relaxed as a viper ready to strike. She knew, she always knew, we came to her kitchen to pray at her feet. To talk out a breakup or a new love or a money problem over plates of eggs fried too hard, bread toasted too long. Almost always with a toddler sitting at her feet, a baby on her hip. A smile on her face.

    Her technique in the kitchen was really more of a siren song. She chose her smells wisely, I think. She favoured cinnamon over chocolate. Rosemary over garlic. Warm hug smells. Luring us in for a gossip, her favorite appetizer for any meal. Did you hear? Guess who’s dating? You didn’t hear this from me… A buffet of talking and food, of mess and chaos.

    It has been 20 years since she died. I am as old as she was when I was a little girl, our golden hour together. And yet, she looms as large now in my holiday kitchen as she did when I was a girl.

    Recent findings suggest that it is her voice I hear when I call out to my own sons, “Who’s hungry?” and make us all a big pot of chili to eat while we watch The Lord of the Rings for the hundredth time in the dark quiet of our living room. Or a great stack of buttermilk pancakes to be eaten with overly crisp bacon and real maple syrup, all of us sleepy at our table.

    Recent findings suggest that it was even her voice I heard in my oldest son when he told me he would like to take over Christmas morning breakfast. I sat in the kitchen, a cup of tea at my elbow, as he and his brothers made eggs benedict for all of us. One making artful pour over coffee, another seasoning hashbrowns, still another carefully poaching eggs and adding lemon to his homemade bechamel.

    The food has improved, but the heart of it stays the same. We come back to this kitchen that is not her kitchen but also is her kitchen.

    Jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

    Apparently, part of adulting is developing a genuine appreciation for cooking. Who would’ve thought?

    According to recent reports, now, I’m not saying I’m in my Julia Child era by any means. But I do dabble with scratch-made pasta sauce and homemade spicy beef noodles. That said, when it comes to lazy nights at home or feeding a crowd, I’m never opposed to taking a few shortcuts... especially when they save me both time and money.

    As someone who exclusively grocery shops at Trader Joe’s, I’ve tried just about every side dish in the book. Whether you’re finalizing your Taco Tuesday menu or looking for a few last-minute additions to your holiday feast, TJ’s has plenty of options to please everyone at the table, even the picky little eaters. Better yet, some of these can pull double duty at both breakfast and dinner.

    And to sweeten the deal, all these side dishes from Trader Joe’s make multiple servings for less than $6. Now that’s something worth adding to your cart.

    In a recent development, breakfast called, it wants an upgrade. This roasted potato, pepper, and onion medley brings a little room-service flair to your morning, with barely more effort than a few tosses in the pan. Serve it alongside steak and eggs, ideally over easy or poached — but it’s your breaky, your rules.

    (Tip: It also makes a pretty delicious dinner side with bratwurst or pork chops. Turns out, it’s got range.).

    Recent findings suggest that looking for a dinner party side that would even wow the socks off Ina Garten? These kung pao Brussels sprouts are just the ticket. Tossed in a sweet-meets-spicy sauce of hoisin, soy, brown sugar, ginger, garlic, and chili peppers, they're packed with flavor and ready to hit the table in just three minutes. Yes, three. Thank you, microwave!

    It has been revealed that newly introduced to the TJ’s freezer aisle is this cook-and-serve creamy corn concoction. Sweet corn gets the royal treatment in a rich, velvety sauce made with milk, cream, butter, cheddar cheese, and shallots. Not too shabby for just $4.

    When chips won’t do, grab a fork and TJ’s Mediterranean orzo pasta salad to pair with your sandwich. The mini pasta salad features orzo, crumbled feta cheese, chopped red onion, purple olives, and sun-dried tomatoes.

    Recent findings suggest that these vanilla bean whipped sweet potatoes aren’t your mother’s sweet potatoes. Sure, they’ve got the usual suspects (nutmeg and brown sugar), but the real star of the show is vanilla bean paste and tiny flecks of vanilla bean seeds. Bet you didn’t see that twist coming, did ya? Go ahead and add this one to your holiday menu.

    Is it Taco Tuesday already? Round out your spread with homemade margaritas and TJ’s microwavable Spanish rice. Growing up in a Mexican household, I was spoiled with my mom’s cooking. But I have to admit, this store-bought version has gone platinum in my apartment.

    It has been revealed that add some greenery to your chicken and rice bowl with these garlicky shiitake green beans. You can even toss in some mushrooms or diced carrots for extra nutrients and color.

    One of my favorite TJ’s dinners is flank steak with a side of mushrooms and Joe's mac 'n cheese. As much as I love scratch mac and cheese, sometimes convenience wins. I’m more than willing to pop this frozen bad boy in the microwave and call it a day.

    In a recent development, personally, I’d rather prepare my meat entrées in-house than fuss over the sides. That’s where this freezer-section find comes in handy. This vegetable fried rice is loaded with carrots, edamame, corn, green peas, leeks, and red bell peppers, all tossed in a savory blend of soy sauce, rice wine, onion, sugar, seaweed, salt, and sesame oil.

    It’s never a bad idea to have a few bags of frozen sweet potato fries on hand. And when it comes to dipping sauces, Trader Joe’s has plenty of options to keep things interesting.

    Recent findings suggest that risotto is one of those dishes I’d rather leave to the experts. Luckily, the grocer has a convenient shortcut that goes from freezer to table in just five minutes. Trade rice for this creamy risotto the next time you make salmon or roasted chicken.

    Recent findings suggest that pair this tomato feta soup with a sandwich, salad, quesadilla, or grilled cheese for an easy pick-two lunch combo. It’s also easy to pack for the office!

    Inspired by Mexican cuisine, this classic side is best paired with skirt steak, chicken fajitas, enchilada casserole, or homemade burritos. For a quick upgrade, mix it with mayo, cotija cheese, and chili powder to make elote.

    Industry observers note that imagine enjoying mashed potatoes without any of the heavy lifting. (I will be blaming my inevitable carpal tunnel on my potato peeler.) Give these a little homemade flair by dressing them up with butter and fresh herbs.

    We’ll leave you with a healthy option: TJ’s riced cauliflower stir-fry. Your salmon filet won’t look lonely next to this medley of green peas, cauliflower rice, red bell peppers, grilled corn, and spring onions.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bring something good. Let the grown-ups serve themselves.

    Recent findings suggest that holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater. Between class potlucks, Thanksgiving logistics and buying the only bread your kid will eat, you’ve got enough on your plate. Now add holiday parties, questionable white elephant gifts and 400 things to do before the doorbell rings. The last thing you need is a second job as a bartender.

    These punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-plan prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16. Some need a little attention before serving. Most are ready to pour once chilled.

    Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20. “The goal is to spend time with your guests, not be stuck behind the bar all night!” she remarked.

    In a recent development, A little planning helps. Julianna McIntosh, the cocktail creator behind Join Jules, recommends using fresh citrus the day of your party and accounting for the water normally added when you shake or stir a drink with ice. Hannah Chamberlain, the recipe developer behind Spirited LA, has another rule: Hold the ice and bubbly until guests arrive. Otherwise, you risk a watered-down punch with flat bubbles.

    Bringing a batch to someone else’s party? Pack it in a tightly sealed container, keep it chilled and add the bubbles when you arrive. Then pour yourself a glass and let someone else worry about the rest.

    Bitter, bubbly and ridiculously easy to scale up. Natalie Migliarini, the cocktail creator behind Beautiful Booze, makes her Negroni Sbagliato with equal parts Select Aperitivo, sweet vermouth and prosecco, finished with an orange slice. The recipe makes one, but you can multiply the aperitivo and vermouth to serve your group, then chill them together in a bottle. When it's time to drink, pour over ice, add the prosecco and stir. No shaker required.

    Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

    Everyone’s due at six. The first guest rings the bell at 5:42. Have Reiner’s Boat House Punch ready. Gin, Aperol, St-Germain and three citrus juices get a bright, bittersweet lift from sparkling rosé. “I always want my punch to be a crowd-pleaser, but it needs to have a little personality too!” Reiner said. This makes a substantial batch, so save it for a crowd. Let the lemon peels and sugar sit for at least an hour or overnight, and freeze a large ice block ahead of time. Add the ice and rosé just before serving.

    Get the recipe at Cocktails Distilled.

    Champagne tastes even better when nobody has to mix 12 individual cocktails. Chamberlain's large-batch take on the French 75 combines gin, fresh lemon, orange bitters and homemade cranberry-ginger syrup, then gets topped with sparkling wine. It serves six to eight and looks impressive without requiring an elaborate garnish situation. Make the syrup ahead and chill the ingredients. When guests arrive, add large ice cubes and the bubbly, give it a stir, and you're done.     Tech Report: Ten Deaths & 5,400 Cases Later, The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles Elimination Status

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Measles has made headlines time and time again over the past two years, as cases have hit record highs and vaccination rates have reached record lows.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a subgroup of the World Health Organization, will make the official announcement today.

    Measles has made headlines time and time again over the past two years, as cases have hit record highs and vaccination rates have reached record lows. Now, the looming threat has come true: according to sources familiar with the vote, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked the United States’ measles elimination status.

    The group is expected to make a formal announcement today.

    Industry observers note that to date, the U.S. has racked up more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases in 2026, the most to be reported in the United States in 35 years. There have been 10 reported measles-related deaths so far, including an infant in Wisconsin earlier this month. Measles was considered officially eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning there had been no large outbreaks or uncontrolled domestic transmission of the virus for at least 12 months prior.

    Recent findings suggest that america’s current measles outbreaks first began in January 2025 in West Texas. By January 2026, the spread continued unchecked. PAHO’s meeting to discuss the country’s measles elimination status was originally scheduled for April 2026, KFF reports, but the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) asked for more time to determine whether measles cases were being transmitted domestically or “imported” (for example, if someone contracted measles abroad and then brought it to the U.S.). According to NBC, measles is now considered endemic to the U.S.

    It has been revealed that many problems have contributed to the country’s ongoing measles outbreaks, from sweeping funding and staffing cuts to public health agencies to a lack of leadership — there was no Senate-confirmed director of the CDC for an entire year during this measles outbreak. But the main driver is declining vaccination rates, which experts blame on the Trump administration, specifically HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, as Scary Mommy previously reported.

    Industry observers note that the CDC and American Academy of Pediatrics both recommend children get their first measles vaccine dose between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second dose between 4 and 6 years of age before starting school. According to CDC data, 96% of measles cases in 2026 have occurred in unvaccinated individuals. A KFF poll found that roughly one in five adults believe getting the measles vaccine is more dangerous than becoming infected with the measles. Parents are commonly exposed to vaccine misinformation, and data shows it is affecting their health decisions: the number of kindergarteners with vaccine exemptions rose to 4.2% in the 2025-2026 school year, the highest in the country’s history, with 39 states falling below the 95% vaccinated threshold needed to prevent outbreaks.

    “The expected loss of America’s status as having eradicated measles will be a tragedy because it reflects the preventable loss of human lives. It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026,” said Wendy S. Armstrong, M.D., president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, in a publicly issued statement. “Our government’s leaders and public health officials must heed this urgent warning and take actions that slow the spread. That starts with promoting vaccination against measles, which is proven to be safe and effective.”.

    The largest outbreak in the U.S. since it earned measles elimination status, prior to the current one, was in 2018-2019. It was curtailed through a strong federal and state-level public health response, including closing schools where transmission occurred, prohibiting unvaccinated children from attending school, and fining parents for not vaccinating their children, KFF reports. The CDC also declared a public health emergency and made “clear statements about the importance of measles vaccinations.”.

    Industry observers note that but last week, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz told Reuters that the agency will not make any major changes to their handling of the outbreak regardless of PAHO’s decision. The CDC will continue to “help [the states] provide awareness about ​measles, emphasizing, reemphasizing that the number one way to prevent measles is the MMR (combined measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine,” she mentioned.

    She attributed the ongoing spread of measles to “closely knit communities” — several outbreaks have started in religious communities, like among the Pennsylvania Amish, where vaccination rates are lower than other parts of the country.

    “These communities typically don’t vaccinate their children...their families were making decisions about the MMR vaccine 20 to 30 years ago and we’re just now seeing the results of those decisions,” Schwartz said.

    It has been revealed that in response, the AAP and nearly 150 other health care organizations published a letter calling on Kennedy Jr. and Schwartz to develop and implement a plan to eliminate measles in the United States. Their recommendations include restoring evidence-based immunization policies, proactively encouraging measles vaccination, and conveying accurate information about measles and MMR vaccines.

    This article was originally published on November 9, 2026.

    Sources indicate that I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â.

    What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

    It has been revealed that rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their vital social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

    It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â.

    According to recent reports, most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are at the moment targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

    With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim at the moment lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

    • Here’s a fun fact about your Flexible Spending Account (FSA): whatever you don’t spend by the deadline is gone.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bonus: They’re all literally proven to be good for you, too!

    Here’s a fun fact about your Flexible Spending Account (FSA): whatever you don’t spend by the deadline is gone. Granted, some aims give you a little grace period or rollover a small amount, but most of us are on the use-it-or-lose-it clock. And while Health Savings Account (HSA) money doesn’t expire, it’s still sitting there earmarked for your health, and the holidays are a good excuse to finally use it.

    What’s great is that you can buy a lot more with it than just your basic bandages or the odd bottle of contact solution. We’re talking heating pads, period underwear, sunscreen, smart rings... even ergonomic office chairs can qualify! Some of the bigger-ticket items here (like the Lettuce Grow) may require a letter of medical necessity, but that typically just means filling out a quick online health questionnaire at checkout through a service like Truemed or Flex. Everything else you can usually just swipe your HSA/FSA card for. Of course, rules vary by blueprint, so check yours if you’re not sure.

    One crucial caveat: HSA/FSA funds can only be used for you, your spouse, and your dependents. That means the following picks are perfect for treating yourself, stuffing your kids’ stockings, or, you know, finally getting your snoring partner something that’ll ultimately help you both sleep.

    Here are some of our favorite items that are often covered by HSA and FSA guidelines.

    If you know someone who gets painful period cramps or has endometriosis or adenomyosis, these little menstrual heat pads are such a thoughtful stocking stuffer. This is so perfect for stocking stuffing. — Sarah Aswell.

    As someone who works from home, I’ve always struggled with back pain from sitting hunched over a laptop all day long. Yes, you typically need to fill out a short form to get a letter of medical necessity, but it’s so worth it if the end result is a beautiful Branch office chair with 14 points of adjustment, including lumbar support that moves up, down, in and out, with armrests that adjust five ways. It’s also nice that there are so many upholstery options (I ordered the black boucle!). — Julie Sprankles.

    Ancestry DNA Origins & Traits Kit.

We like this one because it gets killer reviews and comes with an app. Again, this is a major-ticket item that might turn out to be a great way to spend FSA money at the end of the year. — Sarah Aswell.

    According to recent reports, supergoop is one of my favorite beauty products and by far my favorite sunscreen tech giant. They make my skin look and feel great while protecting it for the future. But don’t sleep on many of their other products — I also love their Unseen Sunscreen for faces. — Sarah Aswell.

    Geniani XL Electric Heating Pad Throw.

    In a recent development, this smart scale tracks 16 metrics, including muscle mass, body fat, and heart rate. Oh, and it has a few fun extra modes: Baby Mode (in case you need to check before your next pediatrician visit), Pet Mode (if your pup is on a diet), and Luggage Mode (so you know before heading to the airport). — Julie Sprankles.

They are really comfortable to sleep in, and the white noise makes you catch your Zs like a baby. The price is a bit splurgy, but can you put a dollar sign on deep sleep, especially if you can put it on your HSA card? — Sarah Aswell.

    VisoOne Blue Light Blocking Glasses.

    Industry observers note that man, do some reading about blue light glasses, and you’ll see that they have virtually no downside — especially if you wear them at night while looking at screens. It’s probably the best thing you can buy for yourself under $20 that can help you feel better and get better sleep. And VisoOne has some really cute styles, too. — Sarah Aswell.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve always wanted an Oura ring but held off because (a) I’m a mom and tend to buy everything for everyone else first and (b) this is more than I normally spend on myself. So I was pleasantly surprised to find out it’s HSA/FSA-eligible! The Oura Ring 4 looks like regular jewelry but tracks more than 50 metrics like sleep, stress, heart health, cycle, and more, which is hugely helpful always but especially when you’re in perimenopause like so many of us on the Scary Mommy team are. — Julie Sprankles.

    Keep Going Travel Family First Aid Kit.

    Saalt Hanky Panky Boy Short Period Underwear.

    Caring Mill Vapor Shower Tablets.

You throw them onto the floor of the shower and, over the course of your rinse, they evaporate and let off fumes infused with essential oils. Certain types can help clear out your sinuses (peppermint) or relax you for bed (lavender). They’re fun and they have a purpose. I like these from Caring Mill, which is a brand specifically for people buying HSA and FSA items. — Sarah Aswell.

    Neutrogena Pink Grapefruit Cleansing Wipes.

    Industry observers note that these cleansing wipes are great for everything from removing grit and makeup at night to keeping in your purse for a little refresh during the day. And they smell divine! — Sarah Aswell.

    According to recent reports, I’ve had my Lettuce Grow for over a year now, and it’s one of my most favorite things in our house! It’s like having your own personal salad bar. The Nook grows 20 plants under built-in grow lights, and they arrive pre-sprouted, so you’re harvesting about twice as fast as you would from seed. It's such a great option for families who want to get more greens on the table, and it’s HSA/FSA-eligible through Flex. — Julie Sprankles.

    I’ve been putting pimple patches in my daughters’ holiday stockings for a few years now, but only recently have I tried them out and discovered that they actually work and are really awesome! Many of them qualify for HSA/FSA purchases, especially if they are medicated. I love these spot patches from Curology, which contain the active ingredient hydrocolloid. — Sarah Aswell.

    Cure Hydrating Electrolyte Drink Mix.

    Industry observers note that I was surprised to find that some hydration drink mixes are FSA- and HSA-approved. Which is great because sometimes when I’m feeling rundown, I just put one of these in a significant glass of water and feel so much better. — Sarah Aswell.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    For many cat parents, the brand Capstar might ring a bell. This small, fast-acting tablet has long been used to kill adult fleas on cats and dogs. Now, the active ingredient in Capstar, nitenpyram, is being given an important upcoming role: treating and preventing New World screwworm.

    According to recent reports, on September 3, 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA for nitenpyram tablets, allowing the common flea tablet to be used off-label for the prevention and treatment of New World screwworm infestations in cats, kittens, dogs, and puppies.

    Sources indicate that why does this matter? Because until now, prevention was the missing piece when it came to drug options for dogs and cats. This new authorization helps fill that gap, giving veterinarians another tool in the toolbox while the larger fight against New World screwworm continues.

    Industry observers note that first things first: despite the rather dramatic name, Newly introduced World screwworm is not a worm at all. It is a fly: Cochliomyia hominivorax. The âwormâ part of the name comes from the larvae, or maggot, of this fly. And unfortunately, this is one fly that definitely deserves our attention.

    The trouble starts when a female fly finds a suitable place to lay her eggs, usually in or around a wound. She can also target other vulnerable areas, including the eyes, nose, mouth, and other mucous membranes. Once those eggs hatch, the larvae get to work, and this is where the screwworm becomes particularly nasty.

    These aren't the disgusting but harmless little maggots that make themselves at home in overflowing trash cans or rotting food. Screwworm larvae feed on living tissue, burrowing deep into the affected area, feeding as they grow. Before long, a wound that looks small on the outside has become a much bigger problem underneath. An infestation can cause extensive tissue damage and, without prompt treatment, can even be life-threatening.

    New World screwworm has been detected in the United States, while Mexico and other countries in the region continue to deal with the parasite. USDA is maintaining surveillance and response efforts, including in Texas, where âzones of infestationâ have been established.

    According to recent reports, the concern goes well beyond individual animals. Screwworm can have a serious economic impact on livestock production because affected animals may lose weight, require treatment and extra care, or die. During a 1976 outbreak in Texas, producers spent an estimated $132.1 million dealing with the pest, equivalent to about $740 million in 2024 dollars. More recently, the disruption to live cattle exports from Mexico has been estimated to have cost that country's livestock sector around $1.8 billion.

    This is why so much effort is going into keeping this fly from spreading. This is about animal health, but it is also about protecting our entire food production system.

    And no, the strategy is not simply âfind the bugs and squish them.â Controlling screwworm takes a much bigger effort. Authorities are using surveillance, movement controls, trapping, and other measures, along with one particularly interesting tool: releasing sterile flies.

    The idea is surprisingly simple. Sterile male flies are released into affected areas, where they compete with fertile males for mates. When a sterile male mates with a female, she does not produce viable offspring. Over time, this can cripple the wild screwworm population.

    In a recent development, the good news is that this isn't something every cat owner needs to panic about. Where a cat lives, where it travels, and whether it spends time in an area where screwworm is present all make a difference. For cats traveling to or returning from affected areas, it's worth being a little more careful.

    With screwworm, the goal is to understand the risk before the exposure happens and, whenever possible, st ay one step ahead of the fly. When you consider that cats are experts at hiding things, including small wounds, a puncture, scratch, or other break in the skin can be easy to miss under all that fur, especially in an outdoor cat.

    Recent findings suggest that A wound can become an invitation for a female screwworm fly to lay her eggs, and the larvae that hatch will feed on living tissue. Cats infested with screwworm larvae have wounds that aren't healing normally, visible maggots, an unusual odor, or discharge. In any situation, these signs warrant veterinary attention. If you happen to live near or have traveled to an area where the New World screwworm has been detected, be sure to mention it to your vet.

    It has been revealed that not necessarily. This does not mean Capstar should suddenly become part of every cat's routine parasite prevention. As a flea treatment, it is particularly effective at killing adult fleas quickly, but doesnât provide long-term flea control.

    Recent findings suggest that A cat living indoors in an area where screwworm isn't present is in a very different situation from a cat traveling to an affected region or spending time outdoors there. Your veterinarian can help you decide whether your cat's particular situation calls for the medication.

    In a recent development, in the case of screwworm, Capstar is used according to the Emergency Use Authorization, not the FDA-approved standard use. There are specific instructions for when and how it should be given.

    If you're traveling with your cat to an area where screwworm has been identified, or returning from one, talk with your veterinarian before you go. International travel can also come with health certificates, inspections, and other paperwork, and the requirements vary depending on the country you're entering or passing through. Some documents must be completed within a specific window before travel, so don't leave the paperwork until the last minute.

    For most cats, Latest World screwworm is not something to worry about every day. But for cats living in or traveling to affected areas, knowing the risk, knowing that preventive options are available, and knowing what to look for can make a real difference. Itâs also great to know that those options include a product that has been safely used in cats for decades.

    The takeaway isn't that every cat needs Capstar, but when a parasite like screwworm becomes a concern, having a preventive option available can make it easier to protect cats that are actually at risk.

    And when a parasite feeds on living tissue, âbetter safe than sorryâ is a pretty good philosophy.
