    #8938. Is It Too Late to Plant Amaryllis for Christmas? Here's How to Get Gorgeous Blooms in Time

    📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (690 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Is It Too Late to Plant Amaryllis for Christmas? Here's How to Get Gorgeous Blooms in Time

    📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It’s not necessarily too late to plant amaryllis bulbs for Christmas, but timing does matter.
    • Recent findings suggest that if you’re growing amaryllis for holiday flowers, choose the right type.
    • Flowering also varies by the plant’s growing conditions, which means you have some control.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s not necessarily too late to plant amaryllis bulbs for Christmas, but timing does matter. Amaryllis typically blooms six to eight weeks after planting, so early to mid-November is your last chance to get bulbs in the pot if you want striking holiday flowers in time for the big day.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re growing amaryllis for holiday flowers, choose the right type. Amaryllis usually refers to Hippeastrum, a South American native, not true Amaryllis, also known as belladonna lilies from South Africa. Most Hippeastrum bulbs sold this time of year are grown in the Southern Hemisphere and will bloom in six to eight weeks. Dutch-grown bulbs take longer, so avoid these.

    Flowering also varies by the plant’s growing conditions, which means you have some control. While early or mid-November is the ideal time to plant a holiday amaryllis, you can do a few things to speed up the process if you’ve just missed the window.

    Getting healthy holiday blooms isn’t just luck. How you choose and plant your bulbs is important. Start by selecting the best bulbs. Look for large, firm, and healthy bulbs without soft spots, damage, or mold. If you see a bulb that has the tip of a green stem emerging, grab it. This bulb has already begun to break dormancy and should flower sooner.

    While unusual varieties can be expensive, you don't need to spend a lot of money on bulbs – Walmart sells preplanted bulbs for under $6.

    Next, choose a good-quality potting mix, such as Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix, available at Amazon, and a container with drainage holes that is only one or two inches (2.5 to 5 cm) wider than the bulb. Position the bulb in the pot so that the pointy end is up and one-third to one-half of the bulb is above the surface of the potting mix.

    In a recent development, water your planted bulb thoroughly, letting it all drain through, before setting it in a warm, bright spot. Keep the potting mix just slightly damp, never soggy. Amaryllis doesn’t need much water and can rot in soggy conditions.

    While you can’t significantly alter the timeline for flowering, a few easy tips encourage strong and steady growth:.

    Sources indicate that you can’t do a lot to force it, but these conditions provide everything your plant needs for a healthy growth rate. Just don’t overdo it. Fertilizer, too much heat, and too much water can do more harm than good.

    Recent findings suggest that be realistic about timing with amaryllis bulbs. If it’s late November, you might still have time for a Christmas flower. Choose the largest, healthiest bulb, with a bit of green growth, if possible, for the best start. Provide the best conditions and cross your fingers.

    In a recent development, if it’s already December, you won’t get a flower by Christmas from a dormant bulb. However, you can probably find a potted amaryllis that has already broken dormancy and has a stem. This plant will likely bloom by Christmas.

    You got some gorgeous blooms in time for Christmas, but now you want them to last. It’s time to switch your care strategy from encouraging growth to keeping flowers looking their best.

    When the flowers do fade, snip them off to keep the plant looking tidy. Once all the flowers are done blooming, cut the stem back close to the bulb. With the right care, you should enjoy healthy, attractive flowers for two to three weeks.

    Here are a few great options available to buy now, with beautiful blooms that will bring a festive splash of color to your home.

    Industry observers note that whether you get flowers in time for Christmas or not, forcing an amaryllis bulb indoors is a great winter activity. Enjoy your blooms, even if they don’t open until January. And if you’re up for it, you can keep the plant going and encourage it to bloom again next year.

    Sources indicate that mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

    #8937. Kate Hudson’s Nostalgic Bow Tree Is Back for 2026! Here’s How to Get the Look – Without It Feeling Dated

    📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Kate Hudson’s Nostalgic Bow Tree Is Back for 2026! Here’s How to Get the Look – Without It Feeling Dated

    📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It's official; Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree from last year is still inspiring holiday decorations in 2026.
    • According to recent reports, it's hardly a surprise.
    • Now, a bow is almost as Christmassy as it gets, whether it’s tied on a tree, a wreath or a present.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It's official; Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree from last year is still inspiring holiday decorations in 2026.

    According to recent reports, it's hardly a surprise. After all, the actress (best known for her starring turns in Bride Wars and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days) kept her Christmas tree simple, classy, and very less is more: think silver, bronze and gold bows, a few ornaments and not much else.

    Now, a bow is almost as Christmassy as it gets, whether it’s tied on a tree, a wreath or a present. A nostalgic tree does have one risk, though: if you do it without thinking it through, it can go from warm and charming to dated really rapidly. Some experts gave me tips on how you can avoid this, and get Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree look.

    For those who have yet to see Kate Hudson's Christmas tree in all its glory, flick your eyes downwards...

    A post shared by Kate Hudson (@katehudson).

    Industry observers note that it feels like a rebellion against the minimalist matchy-matchy (and beige) trend that has been going on for so many years, doesn't it? “People are tired of the same old, store-bought, themed trees,” claims Irena Cara, interior designer and co-founder of Nova Wrap.

    It has been revealed that reilly Renwick, designer and creative lead of State of the Wall, points to Millennial parents whose kids are now the age they were in the 1990s. Many of them, he indicates, want to revive “the warm, festive and childlike vibe of a 90s Christmas, as opposed to what people are now calling the ‘sad beige’ of contemporary tree styling.”.

    So, how best to recreate it? Other than buying some of this beautiful metallic gold ribbon from Amazon. We have a few ideas...

    Hey, we might not have Goldie Hawn as a mum, but when it comes to Christmas nostalgia, a lot of millennials remember our parents' houses being packed with all kinds of stuff, and so much color that it felt cluttered. So, the biggest worry with going with a nostalgic look is the tree looking tacky.

    For Renwick, “the biggest challenge for anyone trying to create a nostalgic tree is how to evade the ‘tacky’ accusations.” His answer is to look at what Kate Hudson did with hers. “The whole point of this ‘comeback’ thing is to evoke the festive vibe of the 90s, not to recreate it in painstaking detail,” he notes.

    Shop Nostalgic Christmas Tree Essentials:.

    Industry observers note that want the Kate Hudson look? “My advice is to use the metallic bows with restraint, in such a way that they stand out but still leave space for the other decorations and the tree itself to still be visible,” says Renwick.

    Recent findings suggest that cara has practical tips for gold, silver, and bronze. “Use brushed or matte ribbon to take the ‘shiny’ edge off, especially if the metals are varying warm tones. Also, make sure the bows are of varying sizes, to keep things interesting.”.

    For quantity, she says: “On a tree between 6 and 7 feet, use between 20 and 30 bows.” Lighting matters too: “Warm white lights make metallics look even better.”.

    A Christmas tree runs the risk of feeling tacky, true, but it can also feel too generic, like it should be in a department store in the 90s. Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a way to avoid this.

    “You can’t purchase nostalgia, but you can tie it!” she indicates. Her suggestion is to reuse ribbon that already means something. “Use ribbons that have a story, such as paper that a bouquet you received came wrapped in. On the loose end of the ribbon, write down the date you received it, and now your tree is a timeline.”.

    Melam preserves flowers for a living, so she also suggests pairing a ribbon with a flower from your own garden. She says you can build the look slowly: “You can add one more ribbon to your tree each year.”.

    If you already have tons of ornaments that have been passed down by family or maybe something your kids have made, bows can tie them into a whole scheme.

    Cara indicates to put the old pieces where people look first: “Place heirloom and vintage pieces at eye level in the center where people look first.” Then, let the ribbon link everything together. “Match the ribbon to details on the older ornaments, such as a gold edge or a red glass.”.

    A big advantage of a bow tree like Kate Hudson's is that it’s very cheap to patch, as ribbon is super easy to swap out for different colors and patterns. “Swap out the ribbon and keep the ornaments to change decorations year to year for a small cost,” claims Cara.

    Melam says to store ribbon carefully between seasons: “Moisture and light will cause your ribbon to fade, so store it flat in a cool, dark, dry place.”.

    Kate Hudson’s tree works because it feels warm and traditional without trying to look like a time capsule. Keep your color palette tight and give your ribbon some history to recreate the same nostalgia.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    According to recent reports, letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, right now home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

    It has been revealed that I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the challenges with stray cats and dogs. I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

    Sources indicate that letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

    Recent findings suggest that in Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

    Sources indicate that the creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

    It has been revealed that our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

    Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:.

    Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source.

    Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity.

    Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety.

    Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior.

    NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership.

    For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

    We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

    We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

    We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

    You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your latest pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

    What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

    Recent findings suggest that everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

    Industry observers note that we would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future. We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

    Industry observers note that A rather significant goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

    We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

    Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

    Sources indicate that some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

    Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

    Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

    Industry observers note that people can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

    If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

    You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

    We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

    What’s That Smell??? How To Tell the Difference Between Normal Stinky Dog Breath and A Warning Sign

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a big difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul.
    • According to recent reports, bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a big difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul. A healthy dog's mouth should have a mild smell, often with a faint trace of whatever they last ate. When that smell suddenly becomes fishy, rotten, or unusually unpleasant, it can be a sign that something else is going on.

    According to recent reports, bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention. Knowing what that smell might be telling you can make it easier to recognize when it's time for a closer look.

    Industry observers note that periodontal disease is the most common cause of persistent bad breath in dogs. It develops as tartar builds up on the teeth and eventually affects the ligament holding each tooth in place.

    It has been revealed that the smell can become particularly strong and rotten as the disease progresses. Other signs include inflamed or bleeding gums, loose or missing teeth, heavy tartar, exposed tooth roots, changes in appetite, difficulty chewing, and pawing at the mouth.

    Sources indicate that gingivitis is an earlier stage of periodontal disease and causes the gums to become inflamed. Bad breath is often one of the first noticeable signs.

    Industry observers note that unlike more advanced periodontal disease, gingivitis is reversible when treated. A professional dental cleaning combined with regular dental care at home can usually address the problem. Without treatment, however, gingivitis can progress into periodontal disease and eventually contribute to tooth loss.

    It has been revealed that sometimes the mouth isn't where the problem starts. Digestive conditions can also affect the way a dog's breath smells.

    According to recent reports, gastroenteritis, acid reflux, food intolerances, intestinal blockages, and even gastrointestinal cancer can all be associated with changes in breath odor. Many of these conditions can cause vomiting, which leaves behind a sharp, sour smell from bile.

    Acid reflux can also produce a similar sour odor even when a dog isn't actually vomiting.

    What a dog eats can have a noticeable effect on breath. It's perfectly normal for some of the smell of a dog's food to linger after a meal, but certain diets can leave a much stronger odor behind.

    Seafood and fish oil supplements, for example, can give a dog's breath a distinctly fishy smell. Dogs that eat feces, whether their own or another animal's, can also develop particularly foul breath afterward. This behavior, known as coprophagia, is unpleasant but fairly common.

    According to recent reports, bad breath isn't always caused by the teeth or gums. The oral cavity also includes the jaw bones, tongue, soft palate, and the inside of the cheeks, and problems affecting any of these areas can produce an unpleasant smell.

    Recent findings suggest that injuries can become infected and lead to tissue damage, creating the odor associated with the breakdown of damaged tissue. Tumors can also develop in these areas and may cause similar tissue damage and bad breath.

    A sweet or fruity smell coming from a dog's breath can have a very different explanation. In a diabetic dog, it can be a sign of ketoacidosis, a serious complication that occurs when the body doesn't have enough insulin and begins burning fat for energy instead.

    It has been revealed that this process produces ketones, which can become toxic as they accumulate in the blood. The resulting breath can have a sweet, fruity smell that is sometimes compared with acetone.

    Interestingly, not everyone can smell ketones on a dog's breath. Differences in how people perceive smells, including genetic differences in scent perception, may explain why the odor is more noticeable to some people than others.

    Kidney disease can give a dog's breath a distinct ammonia-like smell.

    Healthy kidneys filter waste products such as urea from the bloodstream so they can be removed from the body through urine. When kidney function is impaired, urea can build up in the blood instead.

    That excess urea eventually reacts with saliva and converts to ammonia, producing the distinctive smell that can be noticeable on a dog's breath.

    An unpleasant smell coming from a dog's mouth doesn't always originate anywhere near the mouth. In fact, the problem could be at the opposite end!

    It has been revealed that impacted or infected anal glands can cause a dog to lick or nibble the area in an attempt to relieve the discomfort. Anal gland fluid often has an intensely fishy smell, and when a dog licks the area, that odor can transfer directly to the mouth and breath.

    It has been revealed that persistent bad breath is worth investigating rather than simply trying to cover up the smell. The underlying cause could be as manageable as dental disease, but it can also be associated with more serious health problems.

    Regular brushing and professional dental cleanings can help prevent periodontal disease, which is the most common cause of ongoing bad breath in dogs.

    A sudden change in breath odor deserves particular attention, especially if it appears alongside other changes such as appetite problems, vomiting, or repeated licking at a particular part of the body. In those situations, a vet can help determine what's causing the smell and whether anything else needs to be treated.

    In a recent development, as leaves drop in fall, I always wish I’d planted more evergreen shrubs in my garden to give structure and color all through the winter. From tall arborvitae cones to slender columns of holly and perfect no-prune spheres, evergreens give a garden a shapely skeleton on which to hang seasonal blooms. While I’m lucky enough to have mature yew hedges and an old conifer I’m planning to cloud-prune, I want to add evergreen accents to borders and alongside a path to punctuate my garden design. Globes of green leaves in patio planters are high on my wish list too.

    What's stopped me? One of the basic principles of garden design is to always repeat-plant evergreens in odd numbers – and bying multiple plants gets expensive, fast. But Home Depot must have been listening in to my garden-design dreams because it’s not even Thanksgiving yet and a heap of my favorite evergreen shrubs just had their prices slashed in an early Black Friday plant sale. And frankly, the prices were pretty decent even before they went on sale.

    Let’s skip straight to the good bit, shall we?

    Sources indicate that if you’re thinking about planting a privacy screen or hedge, look no further than Emerald Green arborvitae. It naturally grows into a narrow pyramid, reaching 10-14 feet high but only 2-4 feet wide, so you don’t lose too much yardspace or sunlight but get dense foliage to screen your garden from prying neighbors. While many evergreens fade in the coldest winter months, this variety is well known for keeping its bright, glossy tone year round. Thuja occidentalis ‘Smagard’ puts on about 6-12 inches of growth a year so while you won’t get privacy overnight, you won’t need to spend half your weekend pruning it forever more either. Suitable for zones 3-8.

    While most boxwood shrubs grow incredibly slowly, sprinter boxwood lives up to its name, meaning you can buy a smaller, cheaper plant. And don’t worry that Buxus microphylla will grow too substantial because it maxes out at 2-4 feet high and wide: large enough to have an impact in your yard without taking over. Sprinter boxwood keeps its glossy green foliage year-round and has excellent resistance to diseases and pests, including boxwood blight. Suitable for zones 4-9, this handsome shrub is easily shaped to create structural evergreen mounds in a border, a low square hedge or appealing spheres in planters.

    Thuja occidentalis ‘Anna van Vloten’ is a dwarf evergreen that naturally grows in a compact sphere without ever needing to be clipped. With wonderfully textural fan-like foliage, it keeps a bright golden-green tone year-round and grows well in zones 3-8. Anna’s Magic Ball arborvitae only grows to 10-15 inches high and wide and looks delightful dotted through a border. If you’re looking for compact shrubs to boost your curb appeal or want to add some stylish year-round planters to your patio, here’s the easy solution.

    Recent findings suggest that here’s another dwarf cultivar of Thuja occidentalis that naturally grows in a compact ball shape without requiring any pruning. Danica America arborvitae is a little bigger at 2 feet high and wide and a brighter green, but what really sets it apart is its fan-like foliage that grows in vertical layers. The evergreen foliage is denser than Anna’s Magic Ball, too. Use it to create a smart geometric accent alongside a path or add stylish structure to a border without taking up too much space. It's one of the best evergreens for containers, too, and suitable for zones 3-7.

    It has been revealed that for instant style in zones 6-9, few evergreen shrubs have the striking aplomb of sky pencil holly. It’s a cultivar of the lovely Japanese holly and while it grows 6-10 feet tall, it stays a slender 1-2 feet wide with unusual vertical branches. The leaves are small, glossy and dark green – more like a boxwood than a holly – so the growth is dense, accentuating the shape. So, while sky pencil holly doesn’t boast red berries (though it does grow small black berries in fall), its silhouette provides more than enough drama. Happy in a large planter or in well-drained ground, sky pencil holly looks fabulous either side of a doorway or gate, or planted in a loose line, and is one of the best shrubs for a front yard.

    Industry observers note that so far, so green. And while it’s wonderful to have shrubs that bring texture and a year-round skeleton of leaves, some evergreen shrubs also deliver a generous splash of color. And Encore azalea is one of the very best flowering plants to add to your garden in fall. While many azaleas are deciduous, and older varieties only flower for a few short weeks in spring, the Encore series not only keeps its leaves through winter but repeat-blooms all through spring, summer and autumn. It maintains a tidy, rounded shape so requires very little pruning, and there are all sorts of flower colors to choose from. Suitable for zones 6-10, Autumn Royalty has bright magenta blooms and you’ll also find Autumn Lily with white flowers, Autumn Carnation with pink flowers, and Autumn Embers with red-orange flowers in Home Depot’s sale.

    Industry observers note that euonymus fortunei ‘Roemertwo’ is one of those easy wins that every garden needs, requiring little looking after but working hard four seasons of the year. Don't be put off by the fact it's a wintercreeper as this cultivar is a compact mounding shrub. Its evergreen foliage doesn’t lose its variegation and revert to green like many shrubs, and thank goodness because the lime-green leaves have lovely gold margins that positively glow on a dark winter day. Adding to the color, Gold Splash wintercreeper boasts yellow fruit that open to reveal orange seeds in fall. Highly resistant to disease, this neat, ultra-tough shrub reaches 18-24 inches high and wide in zones 5-8.

    Okay, so Viburnum nudum ‘Brandywine’ isn’t evergreen but it does look good all through winter on account of the multi-colored berries that cling to the branches months after leaves have fallen. Brandywine viburnum is one of the best berry-bearing shrubs to feel birds through winter as its berries only sweeten once the worst winter weather sets in, providing a valuable late-season pantry for our feathered friends. Those berries provide quite a show, too, starting green then shifting through pink and blue to a glossy dark purple. Hardy in zones 5-9, this low-maintenance shrub reaches 5-6 feet high.

    Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

    It has been revealed that the path to becoming a professional cartoonist always starts in childhood â pretty much every kid likes to draw, right? And I was no different. Where a cartoonistâs path diverges from that of wiser, more sensible humans is that we love the process of creating more than we chafe at the frustration. Believe me, there is frustration.     Iâve always had a dog until very recently, and had two hilarious knuckleheads as a kid: Shag and Tigger. They were actually father and son, and I didnât need a DNA test to prove it â Shag got out one day, and the neighborhood kids on bikes came by to let me know he could be found down the street at Queenieâs house, where they were in the front yard together. Letâs just say Shag was living up to his name. Then Queenie begat Tigger.

    I grew up in a small lake community, but Shag was found by my grandpa just living on the streets of Detroit. He was pretty feral â Shag, not my grandpa â and impossible to train, but also a total sweetheart. They slept in the garage, and in the morning weâd often find him sleeping on top of the car. Tigger, on the other hand, preferred to sleep behind the toilet. And he wasnât a small dog.

    In any case, I believe these two funny mutts had as much influence on my work as any other cartoonist.

    Great question! Cats and dogs are obviously very different, but they have one really massive thing in common: their own unique personalities. Thatâs what makes both perfect for cartoons â most of us already treat them like little furry people anyway, right? Itâs just their behaviors that set them apart.

    Industry observers note that dogs tend to be goofier, cats tend to be cooler, and they show affection in their own ways, too. Pets generate a lot of material because almost everyone knows a dog or a cat. Even if they donât have one (or many) themselves, the odds are a reader will recognize why the cartoon is funny (hopefully!).

    According to recent reports, one of my most popular cartoons is a sign that states âBeware of Avant-Guard Dog,â and the dog in the yard is wearing black and a beret and holding a sign simply saying WOOF. The idea started as a pun, but I think one of the reasons readers seem to like it so much is that it plays against type. The dogâs sensibility is quite cat-like, making it even more absurd.

    In a recent development, my new book is a full-color collection of the âbest ofâ my dog cartoons from the last decade, and thereâs only one cartoon per page so that they can be seen in a larger format, which was important to me. I put a lot of effort into the art and the details, things that are often lost when the cartoons are shrunk down to an illegible size, so I wanted readers to be able to fully enjoy that aspect of the cartoons. Also, the friend who colors my panels, Ron Raff, is a genius, so whether you think the jokes are funny or not, youâll see that they look gorgeous and consistent throughout!

    According to recent reports, it was difficult but fun to choose which cartoons made the cut, too. Some are simply personal favorites; others were chosen based on readersâ reactions and how much love they got online. Feedback is extremely helpful, by the way â sometimes it feels like Iâm drawing these alone in my belfry studio and tossing them into a black hole, so hearing from people which ones they liked really makes my day.

    It has been revealed that there are two aspects to dog cartoons: The first and most obvious is that they really arejokes about dogsâ behavior in general â how they eat, how they might react in different settings, why they lick themselves, bathroom habits, etc etc. Thereâs a lot of material there! The second aspect is what generates even more material, and thatâs when dogs are reflecting human behavior, or simply behaving like a human.

    Many of the dog cartoons are really about us, and heaven knows people will never stop providing fodder for jokes. Dogs â and animals in general â are a good buffer between the joke and the point of the joke. A good example in the book is a dog shaking a toy in his mouth, and a woman next to him is saying, âBad dog! Drop Mommyâs voodoo doll! Bad dog!â In the background, her husband (presumably) shakes back and forth like the toy. At some level, the cartoon is about the coupleâs relationship, right? But itâs framed by a typical and humorous dog action weâve all seen before. Just not with a voodoo doll, haha.

    According to recent reports, I would say simply that our question is also the answer: love. I try to approach my cartoons the same way I approach dogs in real life; from a standpoint of love, affection, admiration, and a little bit of gratitude that they exist.

    There have been too many to count over three decades! I drew a cartoon years ago of a man walking his dog in heaven, but the leash is attached to the dogâs halo. A few weeks later, I received a card in the mail from a woman whose dog had just passed awayâ¦only a month after her husband. I think of that often: when I share a cartoon, the reader brings their own life experiences to it and then weâve made a two-way connection. That connection is my favorite part of the gig.

    #8930. Breaking: What Your Peace Lily Needs in November – 5 Winter Wins for Glossy Upcoming Growth and Sparkling Blooms

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1783 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: What Your Peace Lily Needs in November – 5 Winter Wins for Glossy Upcoming Growth and Sparkling Blooms

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Your peace lily (Spathiphyllum) may well have spent the early part of fall thriving in its regular corner with little more than a weekly drink.
    • Industry observers note that peace lilies are naturally resilient, but they are sensitive to environmental shifts.
    • Recent findings suggest that by tweaking your habits and pausing unnecessary chores that may have been essential just a month earlier, you can protect root health and ensure your peace lily remains a centerpiece of lush green calm throughout these next few chilly months.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Your peace lily (Spathiphyllum) may well have spent the early part of fall thriving in its regular corner with little more than a weekly drink. But this can all change sharply when November arrives. Suddenly, the lower leaves droop, that trademark glossy sheen can look dull, and the leaf tips might turn dry and brown, even if you haven't changed your routine. The real shift is taking place in the house around the plant, and that’s easy to miss when the plant hasn’t moved an inch.

    Industry observers note that peace lilies are naturally resilient, but they are sensitive to environmental shifts. The days are shorter, the sunlight angles have dropped, and central heating systems are kicking into gear. Good peace lily care through winter is largely about keeping up with those changes. The good news is that the fixes are small. It’s just about recognizing that your plant’s needs change as winter starts to set in.

    Recent findings suggest that by tweaking your habits and pausing unnecessary chores that may have been essential just a month earlier, you can protect root health and ensure your peace lily remains a centerpiece of lush green calm throughout these next few chilly months. Not only will these adjustments protect your favorite houseplant in winter, they will help to set the stage for more striking white spathes come spring. So here’s how to keep your peace lily healthy once the heat comes on….

    Industry observers note that indoor winter living often creates conditions that clash with tropical houseplant health. We seal our doors, turn up the furnace, and seek out cozy, dry warmth. For a peace lily, that same forced-air heating strips ambient room humidity down to single digits while leaving drafty windowpanes ice-cold. Coexisting happily indoors through winter means balancing these conditions, providing the warmth your peace lily needs while protecting it against parched air, dark corners, and soggy soil.

    Diagnosing leaf symptoms early in November prevents minor seasonal stress from escalating into root damage. If your entire plant suddenly collapses into a limp heap, check the soil before reaching for the watering can. If the potting mix is bone dry, a thorough drink will perk the foliage up within hours. If the mix feels soggy and heavy while the leaves hang limp, waterlogged roots are suffocating: stop watering now!

    Industry observers note that brown, crispy leaf tips usually stem from low humidity, uneven moisture, or mineral salt accumulation from tap water. Occasional yellowing on a leaf lower down is normal ageing. However, multiple yellow leaves can indicate insufficient light or waterlogged compost or insufficient light. A long-probe soil moisture meter can help you determine deeper root moisture. I’m a substantial fan of the XLUX Long Probe Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon, which delivers instant readings, so you can address overwatering and soggy potting mix before fungal rot sets in.

    As for flowers, don't expect too many right now. Winter usually isn't when peace lilies bloom. A plant that rarely flowers at all, though, probably needs a brighter spot, unless it's still young (under a year old, some won't bloom yet). Knowing some of the warning signs, hopefully the following tasks will help you avoid calamity this winter….

    Sources indicate that the quickest way to harm a peace lily in November is sticking to a rigid summer watering schedule. As natural day length shortens and light intensity wanes, your plant enters a semi-dormant rest period. Transpiration slows, cell division halts, and roots need less moisture from the soil. A potting blend that dried out in 5 days during July can easily stay damp for 3 weeks in November. Keeping the soil constantly saturated starves roots of oxygen, eventually leading to Pythium root rot.

    It has been revealed that this step is easy: insert a finger a couple of inches (5cm) into the potting mix. Water only when it feels dry and crumbly to the touch. When you do water your peace lily, soak the root ball thoroughly with room-temperature water until it drains freely from the base, then empty any runoff collected in the saucer. Never leave a peace lily sitting in stagnant, chilled water. If your plant droops, check soil dampness first.

    A nifty way of reducing the risks associated with poor drainage is to give your plants some elevation in the drainage tray. Kakuna Plant Pot Feet, available from Amazon, can be inserted between the pot and tray to minimize chills and waterlogging.

    According to recent reports, peace lilies have an enduring reputation as indestructible low-light houseplants, but there is a difference between surviving and thriving. While they tolerate the subdued light of a shaded summer room, the dramatic drop in November’s daylight hours and sun intensity can throw low-light corners into near-darkness. Without help, your peace lily cannot produce the energy needed to support its broad leaf surface, leading to faded foliage, drooping stems, and a halt in flower spathe production.

    Take time now to reassess where your peace lily sits and check how much light reaches the plant around noon. If needed, move the plant closer to an east or north-facing window, where it can absorb hours of bright, indirect winter daylight. Keep the leaves a few inches (8-10cm) back from direct contact with windowpanes, as freezing outdoor temperatures radiate through cold glass and will chill leaf tissue.

    It has been revealed that if placing your plant near a south or west-facing window where bright afternoon sun beams through, hang a sheer curtain to diffuse the rays; direct, unfiltered sunlight can still scorch foliage even in winter. For darker rooms lacking bright exposures, supplemental artificial light provides an easy fix. The GE BR30 Grow LED Light Bulb from Walmart fits a standard socket and lamp fixture, emitting balanced, warm-toned full-spectrum light that sustains photosynthesis through dark winter months.

    According to recent reports, indoor central heating is a double hazard for peace lilies: it strips moisture from the air, while creating extreme temperature pockets. Peace lilies thrive in relative humidity levels between 50% and 60%. When heating systems get switched on, indoor humidity frequently plunges below 20%. This dry air saps moisture from leaf margins, causing crispy brown edges and papery tips. Position your plant away from forced-air vents, radiators, space heaters, and wood stoves. The blast of hot air will promptly scorch foliage. At the same time, keep plants shielded from exterior door drafts and chilly single-pane windows, maintaining a range of 65-80°F (18-27°C).

    It has been revealed that skip leaf misting, which provides only a brief humidity spike and can encourage fungal leaf spotting. Instead, place your pot on a wide tray filled with pebbles and water (keeping the pot base resting above the water line). Alternatively, group multiple houseplants together, or run a small ultrasonic room humidifier nearby. To help you track things, buy a digital sensor like the TempPro TP50 Digital Room Temperature and Humidity Monitor, available from The Home Depot. This compact digital sensor monitors relative humidity and ambient temperature fluctuations, helping you pinpoint cold drafts and heating hotspots.

    During the dark days of late fall and winter, feeding a peace lily does far more harm than good. Because diminished daylight slows metabolic activity, the plant is not producing new tissue or developing roots. Adding liquid houseplant fertilizer during this semi-dormant time means mineral salts can build up in the potting soil. Over several weeks, this salt buildup can burn roots and brown leaf tips. Now is the time to withhold all supplemental feeding until active spring growth returns in late March.

    It has been revealed that similarly, postpone repotting until the warmer, brighter days of spring. It doesn’t matter if you see a few roots poking out of the drainage holes: peace lilies tolerate being slightly pot-bound and recover faster in spring. Moving a sluggish plant into a larger pot now can shock them. The only exception is emergency repotting. If a plant has collapsed from severe root rot, gently tip it from its pot and rinse away old soil. Trim off brown mushy roots with sterile shears, and repot into fresh, well-aerated potting mix. A great lightweight blend for emergency winter repotting is Espoma Organic Houseplant Potting Soil Mix, available at The Home Depot.

    In just a few weeks, broad peace lily leaves collect a fine film of household dust, pet dander, and airborne grease. Dusty foliage can be severely limiting in winter. Dust acts as a barrier, scattering what little winter light reaches the leaves and reducing the plant's already limited photosynthetic capacity. Cleaning the foliage is a quick, high-reward task that keeps leaves breathing and photosynthesizing efficiently. Support each leaf from beneath with one hand, and gently wipe the upper and lower surfaces with a soft cloth moistened with room-temperature water.

    Recent findings suggest that as you clean, inspect the leaf undersides and stem junctions for pests. Dry winter heating can encourage rapid outbreaks unless you catch them early. Bits of white fluff could be citrus mealybugs (Planococcus citri). Flat tan bumps are often brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum). Faint speckling and webbing usually mean twospotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), which thrive in dry, heated rooms. Gently dab mealybug clusters with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, or treat leaf undersides with a gentle organic insecticidal soap or neem oil wash. Bonide Captain Jack’s Neem Oil Spray, available from Amazon, is a brilliant organic way of controlling spider mites, scale, and mealybugs.

    By giving your peace lily a little focused attention in November, you provide the support it needs to navigate the winter months with ease. Dialing back the watering can, finding a brighter pocket of filtered daylight, raising ambient moisture levels, and letting the roots rest will keep the foliage healthy and glossy.

    It has been revealed that set up well in November, a peace lily usually comes through winter looking much like it did in summer, just growing a little slower. The fertilizer and the bigger pot can wait until spring, and so can you. When longer spring days return, your well-rested peace lily will be primed to surge back into active growth, rewarding you with fresh green leaves and a striking display of signature white blooms.

    #8927. Tech Report: The Clever Way to Reuse Old Tomato Cages to Protect Your Plants From Freezing Temperatures

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1271 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: The Clever Way to Reuse Old Tomato Cages to Protect Your Plants From Freezing Temperatures

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wrapped in frost cloth or burlap, an old tomato cage becomes a cheap but effective shelter to protect plants this winter.
    • In a recent development, pulling up tomato plants and stacking their cages in the shed until spring is one of the last big gardening jobs of the season.
    • This trick won't save everything, but for the right plants a tomato cage wrapped in frost cloth or burlap is a smart, cheap way to help your garden get through winter unscathed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wrapped in frost cloth or burlap, an old tomato cage becomes a cheap but effective shelter to protect plants this winter. All sorts of tender shrubs and perennials need winter protection, and temporarily shielding even hardy plants from the worst of the weather can help them thrive. So if you're about to pack away your tomato cages in the shed, stop – they've got another job to do now it's time to winterize garden plants this fall.

    In a recent development, pulling up tomato plants and stacking their cages in the shed until spring is one of the last big gardening jobs of the season. That's a lot of good wire sitting around in the dark all winter, and this trick puts it right back to work. Most gardens have a plant or two that struggles through the cold months, and overwintering plants usually means spending money on shrub covers, frost tents or frames, or insulating zip-up plant jackets built for the job. None of it costs much alone, but the outlay adds up across a whole bed and your old cage can do much of that same work to winterize plants.

    This trick won't save everything, but for the right plants a tomato cage wrapped in frost cloth or burlap is a smart, cheap way to help your garden get through winter unscathed. So, if you're gardening on a budget and wondering how to protect plants in winter, here's the smart solution.

    In a recent development, throw insulating fabric straight over a shrub and it settles right onto the leaves and buds, and cold will seep through wherever it touches. Wet snow is worse. Its weight can bend or snap branches under the cover. But put a tomato cage in there first and the fabric sits on the frame instead, with a little gap between cover and plant. This method also gives you a frame to fasten the fabric to so it stays put when the wind picks up.

    Start with the cage itself. You'll probably find dried leaves and sections of vine still wound through the wire. If last summer's plants had Septoria leaf spot (Septoria lycopersici) or early blight (Alternaria solani), those scraps can carry it over, so pull every one out and disinfect by scrubbing the cage with diluted household bleach and a rinse.

    In a recent development, next comes the fit. Lower the clean cage over the plant and see where the branches end up. Any branch poking through the wire is, more or less, where the fabric will touch the plant later, so the stems need room inside. Push the legs down firmly and, out in an open, windy bed, tie it to a sturdy stake if needs be.

    Recent findings suggest that now wrap the frame in breathable frost cloth or horticultural fleece: one Agfabric frost blanket, available from Home Depot, covers more than one cage. Fasten the fabric to the frame using clips like these stainless steel garden clips from Walmart. Take the fabric right down to the soil as warmth comes up out of the ground at night and a gap at the bottom lets it leak out. Pin the fabric to the ground with galvanized landscape staples like these from Walmart.

    Skip plastic wrap, because the plant needs to breathe and a wrapped cage heats up fast on mild afternoons and damp, still air favors gray mold (Botrytis cinerea). Even without a waterproof wrap, peek underneath every few days and let some fresh air in if needs be. Once the cold snap is over, take the temporary covers off, leaving the frame in place ready for the next weather dip.

    Depending on your USDA zone, the plants that need winterizing in fall aren't just those that aren't hardy enough to survive plummeting temperatures: you can use this trick to extend a crop or protect next year's flower show, too. Ever had a hydrangea leaf out nicely and then barely bloom? Bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla) is the classic candidate because it forms next year's flower buds on old wood, and those buds sit on bare stems all winter. Hard freezes can kill these delicate buds so while the foliage comes through just fine the following year, blooms are few and far between.

    According to recent reports, hybrid tea roses and perennials that are borderline hardy in your zone are good candidates too. If you've planted young shrubs this year – especially if you've been tempted by Black Friday sales on evergreen shrubs and you're planting late in fall – they'll also benefit from being kept cozy during cold snaps. Boxwood and other small evergreens can pick up winter burn from drying wind and sun, and burlap like this Wellco natural burlap roll at Home Depotcuts down on both without pressing on the foliage.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, you'll need to match the plant to the cage size. But if you're planning to upgrade your tomato cages to use a more substantial modular tomato support set-up like these heavy-duty square tomato cages, also from Home Depot anyway, it makes sense to do so now when you can use them to protect bigger shrubs that need a wider frame.

    Sources indicate that once the plant goes dormant, usually after several hard frosts, a sturdy cage can be packed with loose insulation to provide further insulation too. Dry shredded leaves, straw or pine straw like this from Amazon is best. On a bigleaf hydrangea, you can fill right up around the buds, while roses mostly need the extra insulation over the crown and lower canes.

    Keep that fill dry and loose. Leaves raked off a wet lawn and packed tight against living foliage or a crown stay soggy, and that can lead to rot, so let them dry out first before covering with frost fabric. In spring, pull out the fill a little at a time once the worst cold has passed.

    It has been revealed that frost cloth doesn't make any heat of its own, but only slows the loss of warmth rising from the ground at night, buying a few degrees on a clear, still night. In a long, deep freeze, the soil underneath cools off too, and that leaves the cover less and less to work with. Truly tropical plants won't turn winter-hardy inside a wrapped cage, either: hibiscus and mandevilla belong indoors once nights turn chilly, well ahead of frost. In colder regions, some tender plants on the edge of hardiness still do better potted up and stored in a frost-free spot.

    Industry observers note that for most of the year, a tomato cage has one job. But with a cozy comforter of frost cloth, a few clips and a bit of care, this garden staple picks up a second role in winter, sheltering plants that would otherwise need a store-bought cover and helping to ensure another flower-filled year in your garden. When spring comes, unwrap your precious plant, hose off the cage and send it back to the tomato bed. It's the same old cage pulling double duty, and this trick to reuse it over winter barely costs a dime.

    #8925. 8 Things I Learned About Gardening From an Amish Farmer – and Why They're Worth Trying in Your Own Yard

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    8 Things I Learned About Gardening From an Amish Farmer – and Why They're Worth Trying in Your Own Yard

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Some of the best gardening tips never make it onto a seed packet.
    • I recently stumbled across a fascinating piece of gardening history that feels just as relevant today as it did when it was written.
    • Much of what Miller wrote will sound familiar to organic growers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Some of the best gardening tips never make it onto a seed packet. They come from people who've worked the same ground for years and notice what the rest of us walk past – like how a tomato leaf changes color before trouble starts.

    I recently stumbled across a fascinating piece of gardening history that feels just as relevant today as it did when it was written. Back in 2013, Amish farmer Joni Miller sent Modern Farmer a 45-page handwritten essay on organic gardening and farming, packed with diagrams and advice on everything from compost to certification paperwork. All he asked in return was a two-year subscription.

    Much of what Miller wrote will sound familiar to organic growers. Some of it surprised me, though, and it's fascinating to see how well his ideas line up with newer research. These are the eight lessons I found most interesting, and how to use each one at home.

    Industry observers note that miller suggests making a little chart of leaf colors, and I love the idea of reading a vegetable bed that way. For tomatoes and eggplant, he indicates lower leaves that yellow once the plants start bearing give up their potassium to the fruit. A black, rotting spot on a tomato's bottom – aka blossom-end rot – in his experience, means poor calcium uptake.

    Industry observers note that newer research largely agrees, though each symptom has other causes, too. Lower leaves also yellow from a nitrogen shortage, plain old age, or early blight (Alternaria linariae). Blossom-end rot does come from calcium not reaching the fruit, but the soil usually has plenty, and uneven watering tends to be the real trouble. I'd sort that out before buying fertilizer.

    The weed section grabbed me most. Miller noticed foxtail and other grassy weeds sprouting better in tight, high-magnesium soils, and lambsquarters surging after heavy turkey manure. Velvetleaf liked rich ground, Canada thistle faded once soil was loose and cultivated, and pastures full of dandelions never grew lush. As he puts it, "Reading soils by their weeds is an art!".

    Industry observers note that researchers read weeds the same way today, as clues with wiggle room. Weeds tolerate a range of conditions, so dandelions might mean compacted soil and chickweed might mean wet ground, or a neighbor's seed heads might just be blowing your way. Then confirm with a soil test, using a home kit that you send to a lab, like the MySoil Soil Test Kit, available on Amazon.

    Miller's pest advice starts with life cycles, using squash bugs (Anasa tristis) as his example. The nymphs that hatch look like little spiders and start out soft. Each molt hardens them, and by the later ones, he found few organic sprays could touch them. If oil can't smother the eggs, his trick is to "target for those young spiderlings while they're easier prey.".

    Industry observers note that that means turning squash leaves over. Look at the undersides, often in the crook between two veins, and you'll spot copper-brown egg clusters. Duct tape pulls them off easily. If a few nymphs get past you, insecticidal soap or neem oil, like Bonide Captain Jack's Neem Oil Spray, will knock them back, sprayed early or late, when bees are quieter. Adults, by then, are another story, and hand-picking works better on them.

    Straw mulch is nothing new, so Miller's note about greenhouse tomato growers using alfalfa hay caught my attention. It keeps weeds down, but the bigger benefit, he indicates, is that "the decomposing alfalfa feeds the vegetables with high-quality nutrients.".

    Modern studies hold that up. Alfalfa is a legume, so it has more nitrogen than straw and breaks down faster. It holds moisture, too. Once the soil warms, spread 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of weed-free hay around tomatoes and peppers, leaving a gap at the stems.

    Ask if the hay field was sprayed, as some hay herbicides linger, and tomatoes are very sensitive. Can't find bales? Try using alfalfa meal instead, like Down to Earth organic alfalfa meal from Walmart.

    I was surprised to learn you can time weeding with a thermometer. Miller counts heat units. You average each day's high and low, but a high over 90°F (32°C) only counts as 90, a low under 50°F (10°C) counts as 50, and you subtract 50. Weed seeds need about 60 units to germinate, he claims, so he harrows right before that and starts back at zero with each new flush.

    Industry observers note that weed researchers still study the same idea today, under the label stale seedbed, which is a funny name for it, honestly. Simply prepare the bed a few weeks early, water it, and wait for the first weeds, usually a week or two in warm soil. Slice them off in the top inch (2.5 cm) – digging deeper brings buried seeds up to sprout. WaLensee's stirrup-style action hoe from Home Depot suits that shallow work. Then sow without stirring the soil again.

    According to recent reports, this one sounded simple to me, and it is, just about. Miller waters his greenhouse plants in the forenoon, not the evening, and opens the vents on sunny days so plants don't stay damp. Fungal diseases, he warns, "explode in stale, damp environments.".

    Industry observers note that current advice backs him up. Picture tomatoes watered at dusk, still wet at midnight. That's where early blight and gray mold (Botrytis cinerea) get going. Water the soil in the morning instead, space and stake plants for airflow, and stay out of wet rows. Greenhouses need open vents or a fan, and patio pots need elbow room.

    For run-down soil, Miller says green manure crops really help, along with soil tests. Bare soil takes a beating from winter rain. A cover crop holds it with roots and shades out weeds, too. Turned in or left on top, it adds organic matter. Legumes like crimson clover and field peas also pull nitrogen from the air, with help from root bacteria.

    This late in fall, I'd go with cereal rye. Oats and field peas want a late-summer start, and a cold winter usually finishes them off. Crimson clover, available from Outsidepride on Amazon, needs a few weeks of growth before hard frost – unless your winters are mild, that one's an early-fall job. In spring, cut the crop around flowering, before seed sets, then wait two to three weeks to plant.

    Farmers in Miller's community save back their own soybean seed, which he says "helps that variety to somewhat adapt to your farm's soil type." You don't need a farm for it. Save seed from several of your healthiest, most productive open-pollinated plants, not one favorite, and do it again the year after, too. Little by little, your seed comes from plants that thrive in your garden.

    Recent findings suggest that beans, peas, lettuce, and tomatoes are the easy ones, because their flowers mostly pollinate themselves. Squash, cucumbers, and corn need isolation or hand-pollination, since bees and wind can cross them with nearby varieties. I'd skip F1 hybrids, though, since their seed can come up quite different. Dry your seeds well, then store them somewhere cool in labeled kraft paper seed envelopes.

    Industry observers note that much of Miller's letter covers certification forms, buffer strips, and ice houses. But tucked in between are gardening ideas that today's research still backs up. Next season, I'm taking a slower look at my weeds and tomato leaves. You might notice things you've been walking past for years.

    Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success highlights that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    Recent findings suggest that welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a fresh pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral concerns, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine.     Sources indicate that haveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

    Sources indicate that my 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

    It has been revealed that since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

    If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

    I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

    Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

    #8920. The 7 Best Native Perennials for a Garden That Gets More Beautiful Every Year

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1134 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    The 7 Best Native Perennials for a Garden That Gets More Beautiful Every Year

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • They are, after all, the easiest way to create a garden that comes back year after year, growing fuller, more colorful and more beautiful with each passing season, right?
    • No gardener worth their salt wants to start all their hard work from scratch every spring, and why should they?
    • It has been revealed that perennials are especially wonderful plants to build that kind of garden around; if you go native, they can deal with local conditions, making them relatively easy to grow once established.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All hail native perennials! They are, after all, the easiest way to create a garden that comes back year after year, growing fuller, more colorful and more beautiful with each passing season, right?

    No gardener worth their salt wants to start all their hard work from scratch every spring, and why should they? If you can build a garden that gradually finds its rhythm, with established plants returning reliably, filling out their spaces and creating a landscape that feels more natural and abundant over time, it's a no-brainer to make native plants your mode of attack!

    It has been revealed that perennials are especially wonderful plants to build that kind of garden around; if you go native, they can deal with local conditions, making them relatively easy to grow once established. They also offer something beyond good looks, providing food and habitat for bees, butterflies, birds and other wildlife.

    From cheerful summer blooms to delicate grasses, birth month perennials to lush woodland foliage, these seven natives bring a lovely mix of color, texture and seasonal interest.

    Plant them in the right conditions, give them time to establish, and they'll reward you with a garden that gets better with every growing season. You can't say better than that, right?

    It has been revealed that coneflowers are one of those plants that make a garden feel instantly more welcoming. Their daisy-like flowers are drought-tolerant and able to withstand an awful lot of neglect, which shifts them firmly into the almost too-good-to-be-true category of native perennials.

    For a particularly beautiful display, go for the Magnus Purple Coneflower from Nature Hills; it promises substantial bold blooms that never droop, and its flowers attract useful pollinators, while the seedheads provide a valuable food source for birds later in the season, not to mention lots of structure and interest through the colder months.

    If you love a garden filled with sunny color, coreopsis is a wonderful native perennial to consider. Its cheery flowers look delicate, but these little bloomers are tough and incredibly drought-tolerant... even if you're garden gets to that point in the summer when it resembles a frying pan.

    I especially love the Moonbeam (available at Nature Hills), which produces masses of buttery-yellow flowers over a long summer flowering season. Its understated colour makes it particularly useful for combining with stronger shades of purple, pink and orange.

    Recent findings suggest that not every plant in a beautiful native perennial garden needs to produce traditional flowers; sometimes, it's the texture, movement and changing seasonal appearance of a plant that make it special. And pink muhly grass? Well, this pretty cloud-like ornamental brings all three to the table, and then some.

    Bag yourself some from Nature Hills and plant it in a sunny position with well-drained soil. Once established, you'll find that it is relatively drought-tolerant and doesn't require much fuss (so long as you avoid overly wet or poorly drained locations, particularly during winter).

    A beautiful garden needs more than flowers, and an ostrich fern is an especially lovely choice if you dream of adding a lush woodland feel to your yard thanks to its feather-like fronds.

    Unlike the sun-loving flowers elsewhere on this list, ostrich fern (which you can buy at Nature Hills) prefers a cooler, shadier position with consistently moist soil. In fact, like most ferns, it is usually at its happiest beneath trees or along the edges of shaded garden beds, so long as it has enough moisture.

    Bee balm is always an excellent addition to a garden, as its shaggy flowers are packed full of color and nectar, making them very popular with hummingbirds (and therefore a great way to try and lure your birth month hummingbird into play).

    For a native planting, Monarda fistulosa, commonly known as wild bergamot, promises lavender-pink flowers with a fantastic aroma. If you prefer a more dramatic splash of color, the Jacob Cline variety is all about those bright red blooms, while the Spotted Bee Balm does exsctly what it states on the tin.

    Few perennials bring as much cheerful late-summer color as black-eyed Susan. Its golden-yellow petals are basically sunshine in floral form, and they are brilliant for filling out borders in hotter, drier conditions... not to mention blooming for months on end.

    Sources indicate that it grows best in full sun, tolerates a range of soil conditions and is all but catnip to pollinators. Well worth splashing out on something like the Glitters Like Gold Black - Eyed Susan from Nature Hills so you can sit back and watch it do its thing.

    In a recent development, anise hyssop is one of those gorgeous lavender dupes that offers something lovely in almost every respect. It has attractive aromatic foliage, tall flower spikes, a wonderful ability to attract pollinators, and some USDA Zones may find that this one keeps on going until the end of October (especially if you deadhead spent flowers).

    Anise hyssop is a brilliant wildlife-friendly plant that keeps blooming all fall.

    Try planting anise hyssop alongside coneflowers, coreopsis and black-eyed Susans (all of which appear on this list, handily!) for a colorful and super pollinator-friendly border with plenty of height and texture.

    Industry observers note that one of the greatest pleasures of growing native perennials is watching a garden develop over time. Just take care to choose plants that suit your garden's conditions rather than trying to make every plant grow in the same environment if you go down this route.

    It's also worth combining plants with different flowering seasons, not to mention leaving some seedheads standing for winter interest. Over time, you'll find that your garden doesn't just look better for it; you'll also find that it needs less intervention and begins to take on a character of its own as familiar flowers return each spring, pollinators visit throughout summer, and latest combinations of color and texture emerge.

    In a recent development, are native perennials basically a miracle plant, then? Well, no... but they're as close to one as you're ever likely to get! Anything with a 'plant, sit back, relax' vibe to it is always going to prove a winner over time.

    Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.
